_about: Longer 'More about this place' pages, keyed by destination id. Sections: skiing, beyond, know (plain text; *italic* and **bold** allowed; blank line = new paragraph). Describe the character of the terrain, never route instructions. sources: authoritative or local first; if a vendor is listed, list a second.

nagano.skiing:
Nozawa is a proper mountain above a proper village: about 1,000 m of vertical, from tree runs at the top to long cruisers that end in town. Austrian Hannes Schneider demonstrated skiing here in 1930, and a course still carries his name. Snow arrives from the Sea of Japan in long storm cycles, so January and February bring regular deep days, and the beech glades are the local speciality.

Shiga Kogen, an hour away, is a different animal: a high plateau of interlinked areas that hosted 1998 Olympic events, with the most reliable snow in Honshu and a quieter, more domestic feel.
nagano.beyond:
Nozawa's 13 free public bathhouses (*soto-yu*) are run by the villagers, and bathing your way down the main street after skiing is the real après. At the Ōgama spring, locals boil vegetables and eggs in water hot enough to cook them. Try *nozawana* pickles, the village's namesake greens, and soba at a family counter.

On 15 January the Dōsojin Fire Festival, one of Japan's three great fire festivals, has village men defend a wooden shrine against torch-wielding attackers. Near Shiga, Shibu Onsen's lantern-lit ryokan street and the snow monkeys of Jigokudani are an easy half-day.
nagano.know: Stay in a ryokan at least once: dinner and breakfast are included and the bath is on site. Bathhouse etiquette (wash first, no swimsuits, tattoos may need covering) matters more here than in the resorts. The old village is compact and walkable; you won't need a car.

tahoe.skiing:
A dozen resorts ring North America's largest alpine lake, from Palisades (1960 Winter Olympics, the steeps of KT-22) to Heavenly's lake views and Kirkwood's high, steep bowls.

What makes Tahoe unusual is how much **backcountry** sits right beside the resorts: Donner Summit, Carson Pass, the Mt Rose highlands and the Desolation Wilderness above Emerald Bay all have deep guidebook coverage and decades of trip reports. Storms come off the Pacific as heavy "Sierra cement" that settles fast and stays stable, and spring brings some of the most reliable corn snow in the West, often into May.
tahoe.beyond: Truckee's railroad-era downtown, Donner Lake and its pioneer history, Royal Gorge (North America's largest cross-country area), sledding, and the Emerald Bay overlook. Reno is 45 minutes away if you want neon.
tahoe.know: Atmospheric rivers can bring 2 m of snow in days, close I-80, and turn the drive into the crux. Check the Sierra Avalanche Center before anything outside the ropes; guide services and avalanche courses run all winter. Weekends are busy, so midweek is noticeably better.

lyngen.skiing: Summit to sea: peaks around 1,500–1,800 m rise straight from the fjords, and most tours end a few steps from salt water. It's a ski-touring destination first (there are no lifts), with descents above the Arctic Circle in open, glaciated terrain. Late winter (March–April) brings stable spring snow and long days. By late May the midnight sun lets you ski at 2 a.m.
lyngen.beyond: Northern lights in the dark early season, Sámi reindeer herding culture, orcas and humpbacks off Skjervøy in midwinter, saunas and cold plunges, and Tromsø's Arctic Cathedral on the way in.
lyngen.know:
There are three ways to do it, from cheapest to priciest. **Camper van or a rented cabin with a car:** most classic tours start from the road along the fjords, so this is the most flexible way to chase the weather, and how many Scandinavians do it. **A lodge with guides:** in the middle, with local knowledge and saunas included. **A sail-and-ski boat:** the top end, more of a tourist experience, using the boat as a floating hut to reach fjords without roads.

Norway's regional avalanche forecast (varsom.no) covers Lyngen. Weather off the coast changes fast, and planning around it is part of the trip.

chamonix.skiing:
Chamonix isn't one ski area but several, strung along the valley under Mont Blanc: Brévent–Flégère on the sunny side, the Grands Montets above Argentière, Balme–Le Tour at the head of the valley, and Les Houches at the bottom. They aren't linked by lift, so you move between them by bus or train.

The pistes are fine, but people come for the high-mountain freeride. The **Aiguille du Midi** cable car climbs to 3,842 m and is the start of the **Vallée Blanche**, a long glacier descent that most visitors do with a guide. The Grands Montets is the steep, glaciated freeride hill. The terrain is huge and much of it is serious mountaineering ground, with crevasses, seracs and exposure.
chamonix.beyond: A real mountain town with year-round life: climbing history (the Compagnie des Guides was founded here in 1821), museums, good bars and restaurants, and the Montenvers rack railway to the Mer de Glace. The Mont Blanc tunnel puts Courmayeur and Italian food about 20 minutes away.
chamonix.know:
Geneva airport is about an hour away by road. A guest card usually gives free valley buses and trains. The Mont-Blanc Unlimited pass also covers Courmayeur across the tunnel.

The off-piste here is glaciated: if you don't have glacier skills, hire a guide. Bad weather closes the high lifts often, so build spare days into the trip. Midwinter is cold and shady on the valley floor; spring brings long days and the classic glacier runs.

lagrave.skiing:
One old cable car, in two sections, takes you to about 3,200 m on the glacier below La Meije. From there it's roughly 2,000 m of vertical back to the village, and almost none of it is groomed or patrolled. Below the top it's all high-mountain terrain: open bowls, couloirs, cliffs and crevasses.

There are no pistes to fall back on, which is the point. On a good day it's one of the purest lift-served freeride experiences in the world; on a bad one the lift stays shut.
lagrave.beyond: A small, quiet village of stone houses facing the Meije, one of the great peaks of the French Alps. The Écrins National Park surrounds it. For groomed skiing, Serre Chevalier and Les Deux Alpes are close by.
lagrave.know:
Treat La Grave as guided terrain unless you have strong avalanche and glacier skills: getting lost here means cliffs or crevasses. Wind closes the cable car regularly, so plan flexible days and have a backup (Serre Chevalier is about 40 minutes away).

Access is via Grenoble or Briançon. The road over the Col du Lautaret is kept open in winter but can close in storms.

3vallees.skiing:
The world's largest linked ski area, about 600 km of pistes across three valleys: Courchevel, Méribel, and Les Menuires–Val Thorens, plus Orelle and Saint-Martin-de-Belleville. You can ski valley to valley all day without repeating a run.

Val Thorens, at about 2,300 m, is the highest resort in Europe and the most snow-sure. Courchevel has long, beautifully groomed runs and good tree skiing lower down. Off-piste is extensive between the lifts, but none of it is controlled.
3vallees.beyond: Ranges from very luxurious (Courchevel 1850's hotels and restaurants) to simple, car-free apartment villages. Saint-Martin-de-Belleville is the traditional Savoyard village among the purpose-built resorts.
3vallees.know:
Moûtiers is the train station for the valley, with direct TGV and seasonal trains from Paris and further afield. Geneva, Lyon and Chambéry are the airports, all a couple of hours away.

Costs vary a lot by village: Courchevel 1850 is among the most expensive places to ski in the world, while Les Menuires and Saint-Martin are much cheaper on the same lift pass. French school holidays (February in particular) are very busy.

valisere.skiing:
Val d'Isère and Tignes share one big, high area of about 300 km, with lifts up to around 3,450 m on the Grande Motte glacier above Tignes. It's one of the most snow-sure places in the Alps, with a season from late November to early May.

Pistes range from long cruisers to the Face de Bellevarde, the 1992 Olympic downhill. The off-piste is legendary for its variety and is reachable straight from the lifts, which makes it popular and also involved in accidents every winter.
valisere.beyond: Val d'Isère is an old village with a lively après scene; Tignes is a set of purpose-built, mostly car-free stations around a lake. Both are self-contained and very ski-focused.
valisere.know:
The nearest train station is Bourg-Saint-Maurice, about 45 minutes away by bus. Geneva, Lyon and Chambéry are the usual airports.

The off-piste is uncontrolled and the terrain is big: hire a guide or join a group with the local ski schools if you're new to it. Altitude makes it cold in midwinter; spring here is long and reliable.

paradiski.skiing:
Paradiski joins Les Arcs and La Plagne across a valley with the Vanoise Express, a double-decker cable car that swings 380 m above the ground. Together they make around 400 km of pistes, mostly above 1,600 m.

**Les Arcs** has the more interesting terrain: the Aiguille Rouge (3,226 m) starts a 7 km run with about 2,000 m of vertical down to Villaroger, and the trees above Peisey-Vallandry are a storm-day refuge. **La Plagne** is broad, high and gentle, ideal for families and mixed groups, with the Bellecôte glacier on top.
paradiski.beyond: The villages are purpose-built, but some have real character: architect Charlotte Perriand designed much of Arc 1600 and 1800, and they're now protected as 20th-century heritage. In La Plagne you can ride the 1992 Olympic bobsleigh track in a bob-raft with a pilot.
paradiski.know:
This is one of the easiest big areas to reach by train: from Bourg-Saint-Maurice station, a funicular climbs straight to Arc 1600 in about 7 minutes. Geneva and Chambéry are the nearest airports.

Apartments are the norm, and they can be small, so check the size before booking. French school holidays (February especially) are packed. Off-piste is uncontrolled; Météo-France publishes the avalanche bulletin.

portesdusoleil.skiing:
A cross-border circuit of about 12 resorts between France and Switzerland, with around 600 km of pistes. You can ski a big loop through both countries in a day.

Avoriaz is the highest and most snow-sure part, with good parks; Morzine and Les Gets are lower and wooded; Champéry on the Swiss side has the famous Swiss Wall, a long, steep mogul face. Much of the area sits between about 1,000 and 2,300 m, so low snow and rain are real risks in a warm winter.
portesdusoleil.beyond: Morzine and Châtel are year-round mountain towns with plenty of life. Avoriaz is a car-free village built into the cliff, with sleigh rides and an aquatic centre. Lake Geneva is about an hour away.
portesdusoleil.know:
Geneva airport is about 1 to 1.5 hours away, which makes this one of the easiest big areas to reach for a short trip.

Check the snow before you book, especially in early season or a warm spell: the lower villages can be green while Avoriaz is still good. Weekends bring day-trippers from Geneva.

alpedhuez.skiing:
Alpe d'Huez calls itself the "island in the sun": the slopes face south and get sunshine most of the day. Around 250 km of pistes link it with Oz-en-Oisans, Vaujany and Auris, and the Pic Blanc (3,330 m) is the high point.

From the top starts the **Sarenne**, at about 16 km one of the longest black runs in the world. It's long rather than terrifying, and it passes through empty, wild terrain. Off-piste from the Pic Blanc is big and varied, and guides know lines that most visitors never see.
alpedhuez.beyond: Road cyclists know Alpe d'Huez for its 21 hairpins, made famous by the Tour de France, and each bend has a sign with the winners' names. In winter there's an ice-driving circuit, a big sports centre and plenty of nightlife.
alpedhuez.know:
Grenoble is about 1.5 hours away, Lyon a little more. The road up is the famous hairpin climb, so carry chains.

The sun has a downside: south-facing snow turns slushy in the afternoon and icy in the morning, so ski the high, shady runs early and the sunny ones late. Les Deux Alpes and La Grave are nearby for a day of glacier or freeride.

courmayeur.skiing:
The Italian side of Mont Blanc. The resort itself is mid-sized, with sunny, tree-lined pistes that are good on storm days. The big draw is the **Skyway Monte Bianco**, a rotating cable car that climbs to Punta Helbronner at about 3,466 m. From there, glaciated freeride runs drop back towards Italy, and the Vallée Blanche descends to Chamonix.

Treat everything off the Skyway as glacier terrain, with crevasses and changeable conditions.
courmayeur.beyond: A handsome, very Italian mountain town with excellent food, long lunches on the mountain and good coffee. The Aosta Valley adds Roman ruins and castles. Chamonix is about 20 minutes away through the tunnel.
courmayeur.know:
Turin and Geneva are both about 1.5–2 hours away. The Mont-Blanc Unlimited pass covers Courmayeur, the Skyway and Chamonix.

The Skyway closes in strong wind. Hire a guide for the glacier descents unless you have glacier skills and gear. Courmayeur often catches storms from the south that miss the French side, so it's a good backup when Chamonix is dry.

hautroute.skiing:
The classic Haute Route links Chamonix and Zermatt over about six to seven days of high, glaciated terrain, staying in mountain huts each night. Most days involve long climbs on skins, some crampon sections and big glacier descents, mostly between about 2,500 and 3,800 m.

It's a demanding trip: you need solid skiing in all snow conditions, good fitness for several long days in a row, and glacier travel skills. Most people do it with a guide.
hautroute.beyond: Few trips in the Alps match it for scenery: Mont Blanc at one end, the Matterhorn at the other, and a week of high mountain huts in between, each with its own character and a shared dinner.
hautroute.know:
The main season is roughly April to mid-May, when days are long and the snowpack is usually more stable. Huts fill up and need booking well ahead.

Plan for weather: storms can pin you in a hut or force a change of plan, so leave spare days at the end. The SLF bulletin covers the Swiss section and Météo-France the French start.

granparadiso.skiing:
Gran Paradiso (4,061 m) is the only 4,000 m peak entirely in Italy, and one of the most skiable in the Alps. The classic plan is two days: climb to the Vittorio Emanuele II hut, then set off before dawn up the long glacier to just below the summit, and enjoy around 2,000 m of descent back down.

The last part to the summit is a short rocky ridge with a Madonna statue on top, done on foot with crampons. Most people leave their skis at the bergschrund.
granparadiso.beyond: The Gran Paradiso National Park was Italy's first, created from a royal hunting reserve that saved the Alpine ibex from extinction. You'll almost certainly see ibex. Cogne, on the other side of the massif, is famous for ice climbing and cross-country skiing, and the Aosta Valley has fontina cheese and Roman ruins.
granparadiso.know:
The usual approach is from Pont, at the head of the Valsavarenche. The Vittorio Emanuele hut, with its distinctive rounded metal roof, is staffed in spring and needs booking.

The glacier has crevasses, and the summit ridge is exposed. Go with a guide unless you have glacier and crampon experience. Turin and Geneva are both around 2 hours away.

ecrins.skiing:
The Écrins massif is the wilder, quieter alternative to Mont Blanc: big glaciers, jagged peaks and few lifts. The Barre des Écrins (4,102 m) is the southernmost 4,000 m peak in the Alps, and the neighbouring **Dôme de Neige des Écrins** (4,015 m) is one of the classic ski 4,000ers, reached from the Écrins hut via the Glacier Blanc.

Around it, dozens of tours go from huts and valley villages, from gentle glaciers to steep couloirs.
ecrins.beyond: Briançon, the highest town in France, has Vauban fortifications that are a UNESCO World Heritage site. Vallouise and the hamlet of Ailefroide are climbing villages. La Grave and Serre Chevalier are close for lift-served days.
ecrins.know:
The usual starting point for the Glacier Blanc is Pré de Madame Carle, above Vallouise. Huts are staffed in spring and need booking. The Vénéon valley, on the western side, was badly damaged by floods in 2024, so check access there.

Grenoble and Turin are about 2 hours away. The glaciers have crevasses and the terrain is big: go with a guide unless you have glacier skills. Météo-France publishes the avalanche bulletin.

vanoise.skiing:
The Vanoise Haute Route crosses France's first national park, from Pralognan-la-Vanoise to Val d'Isère or Bonneval-sur-Arc, linking glaciers and passes over about five to six days. The Grande Casse (3,855 m) dominates the start, and the route crosses the big, gentle Vanoise glaciers, with optional summits like the Dôme de Chasseforêt along the way.

It's less committing than the Chamonix–Zermatt Haute Route, with friendlier glaciers and easier days, which makes it a good first big traverse.
vanoise.beyond: The huts are traditional and welcoming, and there's a good chance of seeing ibex and chamois. Bonneval-sur-Arc, at the end, is one of the most beautiful stone villages in the French Alps. Beaufort cheese comes from these valleys.
vanoise.know:
Spring (roughly March to May) is the season, when huts are staffed. Book ahead. The start is about 2.5 hours from Geneva or Chambéry; arrange the return from the finish in advance.

You need glacier travel skills and gear, or a guide. Météo-France publishes the avalanche bulletin.

maira.skiing:
Valle Maira, in Piedmont near the French border, has no lifts at all and hundreds of mapped ski tours. From each hamlet, you can choose open slopes, wooded ridges and steeper couloirs, mostly between about 1,500 and 3,000 m.

The valley catches storms from the south and the Mediterranean, so its snow can be very different from the northern Alps, for better or worse. In a good year it's a touring paradise.
maira.beyond:
Valle Maira is part of the Occitan world, with its own language, music and food. Small guesthouses (*locande*) in stone hamlets offer half-board, and the cooking is a big part of the trip: local ravioli, polenta, cheeses and Piedmont wines like Barolo.

The valley lost most of its population in the 20th century, and its revival is partly thanks to slow, low-impact tourism like this.
maira.know:
Turin is about 2 hours away, and Cuneo is the nearest town. A car is the easiest way to get around.

Snow varies a lot from year to year. Check the Piedmont avalanche bulletin (ARPA Piemonte). Local guides know the best tours for the conditions.

verbier.skiing:
Verbier is the hub of the 4 Vallées, a linked area of about 400 km that also takes in Nendaz, Veysonnaz, Thyon and La Tzoumaz. The pistes are good, but Verbier's reputation is freeride: steep, varied off-piste is reachable straight from the lifts, from the top of Mont Fort (3,330 m) down.

The Bec des Rosses face hosts the Xtreme Verbier, the final of the Freeride World Tour. Much of the best terrain is ungroomed 'itinéraire' runs and off-piste, so conditions vary a lot day to day.
verbier.beyond: A chalet village with a big international crowd and one of the liveliest nightlife scenes in the Alps. Quieter villages around the 4 Vallées are cheaper bases. The Rhône valley below has vineyards and the thermal baths at Saillon and Lavey.
verbier.know:
Le Châble, in the valley, has a train station and a cable car up to Verbier, so you can arrive by train from Geneva (about 2 hours). Verbier is expensive, especially in high season.

The off-piste is popular, which means tracked out fast after storms and involved in accidents every winter. A local guide finds the good snow and keeps you out of trouble.

zermatt.skiing:
Zermatt is skiing under the Matterhorn, and the mountain is in view from almost every run. Three sectors (Sunnegga–Rothorn, Gornergrat and the Matterhorn Glacier Paradise) climb to 3,883 m, the highest cable-car station in Europe, with glacier skiing even in summer. Across the Theodul glacier, the lifts connect to **Cervinia** in Italy, so you can ski over the border for lunch.

The pistes are long and high, with lots of vertical. Off-piste around the Stockhorn and Schwarzsee is excellent but glaciated in places, so a guide is a good idea.
zermatt.beyond:
The village is car-free, with electric taxis and horse-drawn sleighs. The mountain restaurants are some of the best in the Alps, and long lunches on a sunny terrace are part of the culture. The Matterhorn Museum tells the story of the first ascent in 1865, which ended in tragedy on the way down.

The Gornergrat railway, opened in 1898, climbs to a famous viewpoint over the Monte Rosa glaciers.
zermatt.know:
Arrive by train: change at Visp, or park in Täsch and take the shuttle train. Zurich and Geneva are about 3.5 hours away. The Glacier Express connects to St. Moritz.

Zermatt is expensive. The international pass is needed for Cervinia. High winds close the top lifts and the link to Italy. The SLF publishes the Swiss avalanche bulletin.

saasfee.skiing:
Saas-Fee sits in a bowl surrounded by thirteen peaks over 4,000 m, with the Fee glacier hanging right above the village. The skiing is high and snow-sure, reaching about 3,500 m on the Allalin glacier via the **Metro Alpin**, an underground funicular. National ski teams train on the glacier in autumn.

The pistes are mostly intermediate and the off-piste is limited by crevasses. For tourers, the Allalinhorn (4,027 m) is one of the most accessible 4,000 m summits in the Alps, starting from the top of the Metro Alpin.
saasfee.beyond: The village is car-free and quieter than Zermatt. At the top of the Metro Alpin, the Mittelallalin has a revolving restaurant and an ice pavilion carved into the glacier. The other villages of the Saas valley (Saas-Grund and Saas-Almagell) are cheaper and calmer.
saasfee.know:
Take the train to Visp, then the bus up the valley. Geneva and Zurich are around 3 hours away.

Altitude gives a long season, from November to April. The glacier has crevasses, so stay on the pistes unless you're with a guide. The SLF publishes the avalanche bulletin.

engelberg.skiing:
Engelberg is a low village under a high mountain: the **Titlis** (3,020 m) rises about 2,000 m above town. The Laub is a huge, steep open face of about 1,000 m vertical, and the Galtiberg is a long descent of around 2,000 m from the glacier to the valley. Both are classic big-mountain lines that are reachable by lift.

The pistes are modest; the freeride is the reason to come.
engelberg.beyond: A strong Scandinavian freeride community (mostly Swedish) has settled here, bringing bars, guides and a lively scene. The Benedictine abbey, founded in the 12th century, has a show cheese dairy. Lucerne is about 45 minutes away by train.
engelberg.know:
Zurich is about 1.5 hours away by train. The Rotair, a rotating cable car, climbs to the Titlis summit.

The low village means rain is possible at the bottom when it snows at the top. The big lines are serious avalanche and glacier terrain, with crevasses on the upper slopes. Go with a guide, and check the SLF bulletin.

andermatt.skiing:
The **Gemsstock** (2,961 m) above Andermatt is one of the best freeride mountains in Switzerland, with steep north-facing bowls and couloirs and about 1,500 m of vertical. Andermatt sits at a weather crossroads near the Gotthard, catching storms from both north and south.

The Oberalp pass links Andermatt with Sedrun and Disentis into one area, with good off-piste on the Disentis side too.
andermatt.beyond: Andermatt used to be a quiet army garrison town. In recent years, a big resort development, now partly owned by Vail Resorts, has added hotels and apartments. The old village still has charm, and the Devil's Bridge in the Schöllenen gorge is linked to a famous Russian army crossing in 1799.
andermatt.know:
Zurich is about 2 hours away by train. The Matterhorn Gotthard railway, including the Glacier Express, links the area.

The Gemsstock is serious avalanche terrain, and the snowpack can be tricky after big storms. Go with a guide, and check the SLF bulletin.

engadin.skiing:
The Engadin is a high, sunny valley at around 1,800 m, with St. Moritz and Pontresina as its main villages. **Corviglia** has wide, sunny pistes; **Corvatsch** is higher, steeper and more snow-sure; and **Diavolezza** offers a long run down the Morteratsch glacier with a guide.

The climate is dry and sunny, so the snow is often cold and fast, but the snowpack can be weak.
engadin.beyond:
St. Moritz hosted the Winter Olympics in 1928 and 1948, and has an extravagant winter culture: the Cresta Run toboggan, the natural-ice bobsleigh track and horse racing on the frozen lake (White Turf). The Engadin Ski Marathon in March is one of the biggest cross-country races in the world.

Romansh is spoken here, and the valley's villages have beautiful painted houses.
engadin.know:
Zurich is about 3 to 3.5 hours away by train, via the UNESCO-listed Albula line. The Bernina Express runs south to Italy.

St. Moritz is very expensive, but Pontresina and the smaller villages are better value. The inner-Alpine snowpack can be weak, so be careful off-piste and check the SLF bulletin.

davos.skiing:
Davos and Klosters share five ski areas, and the best is the **Parsenn**, with long runs to valley villages like Küblis, a descent of about 12 km. Jakobshorn, Pischa, Rinerhorn and Madrisa add variety, from freestyle parks to quiet off-piste.

The off-piste is big and varied, and the long runs to the valley are a highlight.
davos.beyond:
Davos is the highest town in Europe and home to the World Economic Forum. Thomas Mann set *The Magic Mountain* in one of its sanatoriums. Klosters is a smaller, quieter village, a favourite of the British royal family. The Spengler Cup ice hockey tournament takes place over Christmas.

The SLF, Switzerland's avalanche research institute, is based here, and publishes the Swiss bulletin.
davos.know:
Zurich is about 2 to 2.5 hours away by train. The ski areas aren't linked, so you move between them by bus or train.

The inner-Alpine snowpack can be weak. Check the SLF bulletin and go with a guide off-piste.

laax.skiing:
Laax is Europe's freestyle capital, with huge terrain parks and one of the biggest halfpipes in the world. It hosts the Laax Open, a major snowboard and freeski event. Beyond the parks, Laax, Flims and Falera share around 225 km of pistes, with wide open slopes up to the Vorab glacier at about 3,000 m.

The freeride is good and varied, with lots of terrain between the lifts.

Laax is also known for its innovations, from early adoption of snowboarding to its app-based lift system. The parks are open to all levels, with lines for beginners and experts.
laax.beyond: The Flims rockslide, one of the biggest in the Alps, shaped the landscape and carved the Rhine Gorge (Ruinaulta), sometimes called the "Swiss Grand Canyon". The Caumasee lake is beautiful year-round. The Rocks Resort, at the Laax base, has a modern, urban vibe.
laax.know:
Zurich is about 1.5 to 2 hours away, by train to Chur then bus.

The Vorab glacier has crevasses off-piste. The SLF publishes the avalanche bulletin.

jungfrau.skiing:
Wengen, Grindelwald and Mürren sit under the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau, and the scenery is the point. The pistes are mostly intermediate and fairly low, but the views are among the best in the Alps.

Wengen hosts the **Lauberhorn**, the longest downhill on the World Cup circuit. Mürren is home to the **Inferno**, one of the biggest amateur ski races in the world, held since 1928. Off-piste is limited but good above Mürren, around the Schilthorn.
jungfrau.beyond: The Schilthorn's revolving restaurant, Piz Gloria, appeared in the James Bond film *On Her Majesty's Secret Service*. The Jungfraujoch railway climbs through the Eiger to the highest railway station in Europe. Sledging is a big part of the culture here, with long runs from the Faulhorn and elsewhere.
jungfrau.know:
Wengen and Mürren are car-free. Take the train from Interlaken; Zurich and Bern are 1.5 to 2.5 hours away. The Eiger Express gondola links Grindelwald to the ski area.

The lower slopes can be thin in a warm winter. The SLF publishes the avalanche bulletin.

monterosa.skiing:
Monterosa Ski links three valleys (Alagna in the Valsesia, Gressoney and Champoluc) on the Italian side of Monte Rosa. Alagna is the freeride mecca: few pistes, but huge, lift-served off-piste with long descents through steep faces and couloirs.

Heli-skiing is legal in Italy (unlike in France), so heli drops reach glaciers on Monte Rosa that would otherwise take hours to climb.
monterosa.beyond: Alagna is a Walser village, settled centuries ago by German-speaking farmers who built distinctive wooden houses. The Capanna Margherita, on a 4,554 m summit of Monte Rosa, is the highest hut in Europe. The food is hearty: polenta, fontina and Piedmont wines.
monterosa.know:
Milan and Turin are about 2 hours away. Alagna is the place for freeride; Gressoney and Champoluc are better for pistes and families.

The terrain is big and the glaciers have crevasses: go with a local guide. Storms from the south can bring heavy snow that the northern Alps miss.

bernese.skiing:
The Bernese Oberland Haute Route starts with a train ride through the Eiger to the Jungfraujoch (3,454 m), then tours across the Aletsch glacier world: the largest glacier in the Alps and a UNESCO World Heritage site. Huts such as Konkordia and Finsteraarhorn are bases for big summits like the Finsteraarhorn (4,274 m), the highest in the Bernese Alps.

The usual exit is over a high pass into the Lötschental or down to Fiesch.
bernese.beyond: The Konkordia hut sits on a cliff high above the glacier, reached by hundreds of metal steps, because the glacier has thinned so much since the hut was built. It's a striking reminder of how fast the Alps are changing.
bernese.know:
Spring (roughly March to May) is the season. Book huts ahead.

The train takes you straight to 3,454 m without acclimatisation, so the first night can be hard. You need glacier skills and gear, or a guide. The SLF publishes the avalanche bulletin.

arlberg.skiing:
The Arlberg links St. Anton, St. Christoph, Stuben, Lech, Zürs and Warth-Schröcken into one of the biggest areas in Austria, with around 300 km of runs. It's known for steep, challenging terrain and for its **ski routes**: marked, avalanche-controlled runs that are never groomed, somewhere between a piste and off-piste.

The off-piste from the Valluga and around Lech and Zürs is huge, varied and among the best lift-served freeride in the Alps.
arlberg.beyond: The Arlberg is where modern ski technique and teaching began, in the early 20th century. St. Anton has one of the liveliest après scenes in the Alps; Lech and Zürs are quieter and more exclusive, with excellent hotels and restaurants.
arlberg.know:
St. Anton has its own train station on the main line between Zurich and Innsbruck, about 2.5 hours from Zurich and 1 hour from Innsbruck.

Lech limits how many day passes it sells, which keeps it uncrowded. The ski routes aren't patrolled like pistes, and the off-piste is uncontrolled: go with a guide to explore. It's a very snowy area, and avalanche danger can be high after storms.

ischgl.skiing:
The Silvretta Arena links Ischgl in Austria with Samnaun in Switzerland into about 240 km of pistes, almost all above 2,000 m. The hub is the Idalp, a broad high basin, and from there long, wide reds fan out in every direction, including over the border to Switzerland. It's a confident intermediate's playground, with good off-piste between the lifts on a powder day.

Altitude is the selling point: the season runs reliably from late November to early May.
ischgl.beyond:
Ischgl is famous for partying, from afternoon après to clubs that run late, and for the free "Top of the Mountain" concerts that open and close the season. Samnaun, on the Swiss side, is duty-free, and people ski over to stock up.

Galtür, further up the Paznaun valley, is the quiet alternative. In 1999 a huge avalanche hit the village and killed 31 people; the Alpinarium, built into the new protection wall, tells the story.
ischgl.know:
Innsbruck is about 1.5 hours away; Landeck is the nearest train station, with buses up the valley. Ischgl is busy and not cheap, especially in high season. Staying in Galtür or Kappl and taking the bus is calmer and better value.

The inner-Alpine snowpack can be weak in thin winters, so be careful off-piste and check the Tyrol avalanche bulletin.

otztal.skiing:
Two very different resorts share one long valley. **Sölden** is big, lively and high, with two glaciers (Rettenbach and Tiefenbach) and its "Big 3": three peaks above 3,000 m, each with a viewing platform. The World Cup season opens on the Rettenbach glacier every October.

**Obergurgl-Hochgurgl**, at the head of the valley, sits at about 1,900 m and is one of the most snow-sure resorts in Austria. The terrain is mostly easy and intermediate, quiet and sunny, with good touring right from the lifts.
otztal.beyond: Sölden is a party town; Obergurgl is calm and family-oriented. On the Gaislachkogl summit, the glass-walled ice Q restaurant was a set for the Bond film *Spectre*, and the 007 Elements exhibition sits next to it. Hochgurgl has a motorcycle museum at the top of the closed Timmelsjoch pass road. The Aqua Dome thermal spa in Längenfeld is the classic rest day.
otztal.know:
About 1 hour from Innsbruck by car or bus. Obergurgl and Sölden are on different lift passes, though combined passes exist.

The glaciers make early and late season possible, but they close in strong wind. Off-piste is uncontrolled and the inner-Alpine snowpack is often weak; check the Tyrol bulletin.

kitzbuhel.skiing:
Kitzbühel's KitzSki area covers around 230 km of pistes on several mountains around a medieval town, and the neighbouring SkiWelt Wilder Kaiser–Brixental adds a similar amount more. The runs are long, varied and mostly intermediate, with mountain huts at every turn.

The **Streif**, home of the Hahnenkamm downhill each January, is the most famous race course in the world: the Mausefalle jump at the top drops racers onto an 85% slope. You can ski most of it yourself, on a gentler route around the steepest sections.

The area is fairly low, mostly under 2,000 m, so snowmaking matters and the season can be short in a warm winter.
kitzbuhel.beyond: The pedestrian old town has painted houses, good shops, restaurants and nightlife. Toni Sailer, who won three Olympic golds in 1956, was a local hero. Hahnenkamm weekend is one of the biggest parties in skiing.
kitzbuhel.know:
Salzburg and Innsbruck are about 1 hour away, Munich about 1.5 hours, and the town has its own train station.

Check the snow before booking early or late in the season. January race week is busy and expensive.

zillertal.skiing:
The Zillertal is a valley of several ski areas covered by one pass, with more than 500 km of pistes in total. **Mayrhofen** has the Penken and the **Harakiri**, with a gradient of 78%, the steepest groomed run in Austria. **Hintertux**, at the head of the valley, has glacier skiing up to about 3,250 m, open all year.

The Zillertal Arena, Hochfügen and Hochzillertal add plenty of variety. Hochfügen is especially good for freeride.
zillertal.beyond: The valley towns are lively, with lots of après. Inside the Hintertux glacier, the Natur Eis Palast is a cave you can tour, with ice formations and an underground lake. The Snowbombing festival takes over Mayrhofen each April. Innsbruck is close for a city day.
zillertal.know:
Jenbach is the main train station, about 1 hour from Innsbruck, with the Zillertalbahn running up the valley. Ski buses link the areas, but a car helps.

The lower areas can be thin in a warm winter, but Hintertux almost always has snow. Off-piste is uncontrolled; check the Tyrol bulletin.

saalbach.skiing:
The Skicircus links Saalbach, Hinterglemm, Leogang and Fieberbrunn into about 270 km of pistes. You can ski a full circuit around the valley in either direction, which makes it great for intermediates who like to cover distance and never repeat a run.

Fieberbrunn, linked in more recently, catches more snow than the rest and hosts a Freeride World Tour stop on the Wildseeloder. Saalbach hosted the Alpine World Ski Championships in 2025.
saalbach.beyond: This is one of the great après valleys of Austria, with busy mountain huts, umbrella bars and live music from mid-afternoon. Zell am See, with its frozen lake and the Kitzsteinhorn glacier above Kaprun, is close for a change of scenery.
saalbach.know:
Salzburg is about 1.5 hours away. The area is mid-altitude, mostly below about 2,100 m, so conditions vary with the winter; snowmaking is extensive. If the Skicircus is thin, the Kitzsteinhorn glacier nearby is a good backup.

Good value for a big area, and popular with groups. Off-piste is uncontrolled; check the Salzburg and Tyrol bulletins.

dolomiti.skiing:
Dolomiti Superski is one pass covering about 12 valleys and around 1,200 km of pistes, including Val Gardena, Alta Badia, Arabba and Cortina d'Ampezzo. The **Sella Ronda** is the classic: a loop around the Sella massif, skiable in either direction in a day.

The skiing is mostly groomed and intermediate, among dramatic pale limestone towers. The Marmolada glacier and the long run through the Hidden Valley from Lagazuoi are highlights.
dolomiti.beyond: The food is a big part of the trip: mountain huts serve excellent South Tyrolean and Italian cooking, and Alta Badia has several Michelin-starred restaurants. The Ladin culture, the open-air WWI museums along the old front line, and Cortina (an Olympic host in 1956 and 2026) add depth.
dolomiti.know:
Venice, Verona and Innsbruck are 2 to 3 hours away. A car helps, though buses link the valleys.

Natural snowfall can be thin, but snowmaking is excellent and the pistes are usually in great shape. Off-piste is limited and often steep and rocky: the Dolomites are a groomed-skiing and touring destination more than a freeride one.

livigno.skiing:
Livigno sits at about 1,800 m in a remote valley near the Swiss border, so it's cold and snow-sure. Two sides of the valley, **Mottolino** and **Carosello 3000**, offer about 115 km of mostly wide, open intermediate pistes, and Mottolino's terrain park is one of the best in Europe.

Livigno hosted the freestyle and snowboard events of the 2026 Winter Olympics.
livigno.beyond: Livigno has long been duty-free, so fuel, alcohol and electronics are cheap, and the long main street is lined with shops. It's a lively, young town. Bormio, over the pass, has thermal baths dating back to Roman times.
livigno.know:
Remote to reach: about 3 to 3.5 hours from Milan or Zurich. From Switzerland, a narrow, one-lane toll tunnel (the Munt la Schera) runs in alternating directions; from Italy, a high pass can close in storms.

The altitude makes it bitterly cold in midwinter, and spring is pleasant. Off-piste is uncontrolled; check the Lombardy avalanche bulletin.

silvretta.skiing:
Gentle, glaciated hut touring on the border between Austria and Switzerland, with lots of peaks around 3,000 m. Big huts such as the **Jamtalhütte** and **Wiesbadener Hütte** make good bases, and Piz Buin (3,312 m), the peak that gave the sunscreen its name, is the best-known summit. The Dreiländerspitze, where Tyrol, Vorarlberg and Switzerland meet, is another classic.

The terrain is friendlier than many high Alpine areas, which makes it a good first hut trip, though the glaciers still need care.
silvretta.beyond: The huts are comfortable by Alpine standards, with good food and a sociable atmosphere. The **Rätikon**, to the west, adds limestone peaks, the Drei Türme and the Lünersee, with a different, more Dolomite-like feel.
silvretta.know:
The usual starting points are Galtür, in the Paznaun valley, and the Montafon. The Silvretta high road is closed in winter. Huts are staffed in spring (roughly February to May) and need booking, especially at Easter.

Glacier skills or a guide are needed for the higher tours. Check the Tyrol and Vorarlberg avalanche bulletins.

otztalhuts.skiing:
High, glaciated hut touring from Vent, a small village at about 1,900 m at the head of the Ötztal. The huts (the Breslauer, the Vernagthütte, the Hochjochhospiz and the high Brandenburger Haus) sit among some of the biggest glaciers in Austria. The **Wildspitze** (3,768 m), Austria's second-highest peak, is the classic summit.

Days are long, with big glacier crossings, and the terrain is more serious than the Silvretta or Stubai, with greater distances and altitude. A popular plan is to cross into Italy via the Similaun.
otztalhuts.beyond: Ötzi, the 5,000-year-old iceman, was found on a glacier pass near the Similaun hut in 1991. Every summer, shepherds still drive sheep across the glaciers between Italy and the Ötztal, a tradition recognised by UNESCO. Vent is tiny and quiet, and the Aqua Dome spa down the valley is a good finish.
otztalhuts.know:
Spring (roughly March to May) is the season. Book huts ahead. You need glacier skills, crampons and good fitness, or a guide.

About 1.5 hours from Innsbruck. The inner-Alpine snowpack can be weak; check the Tyrol bulletin daily.

stubai.skiing:
The Stubai Alps have one of the densest hut networks in Austria, and they're the classic place for a first hut-touring week. The **Franz-Senn-Hütte**, named after a priest who helped found the Alpine Club, and the **Amberger Hütte** are bases for many 3,000 m peaks. You can tour from one hut for several days or link several huts together.

The Zuckerhütl (3,507 m) is the highest summit. The Stubai Glacier, Austria's largest glacier ski area, is close for a warm-up day on lifts.
stubai.beyond: Innsbruck is less than an hour away, so a city day is easy. The huts are traditional and welcoming, with hearty Tyrolean food like Kaspressknödel (cheese dumplings).
stubai.know:
Spring is the main season. Book huts ahead, especially at weekends and Easter. Buses run from Innsbruck into the Stubai valley.

The terrain mixes glaciers and steep slopes, so glacier skills or a guide are needed. The Tyrol bulletin covers the area.

ortler.skiing:
High, glaciated touring in the Stelvio National Park, around the Ortler and Cevedale groups. The **Casati hut**, at about 3,250 m on the pass below the Cevedale, and the **Branca hut** in the Forni valley are the classic bases. From them, big rounded glacier summits like the Cevedale (3,769 m) and Palon de la Mare (3,703 m) make some of the best ski 3,000ers in the Alps.

The Ortler itself (3,905 m) is more of a mountaineering objective. The altitude keeps the snow good late into spring.
ortler.beyond: This area was on the front line of the First World War, the so-called "White War" fought on glaciers, and the melting ice still reveals traces of it. Bormio, with its Roman thermal baths, is the place to recover.
ortler.know:
Spring (roughly March to May) is the season. Access is from Santa Caterina Valfurva or Solda. Milan is about 3.5 hours away; the Stelvio pass is closed in winter.

You need glacier skills, crampons and acclimatisation for the altitude, or a guide. Check the Lombardy and South Tyrol avalanche bulletins.

fanes.skiing:
Quieter Dolomites touring through the Fanes-Senes-Braies nature park, between Cortina and Alta Badia: high limestone plateaus, gentle valleys and some steeper peaks. Rifugi such as **Fanes**, **Lavarella** and **Sennes** make bases for day tours or a multi-day traverse, with summits like Col Becchei and Piz Lavarella.

The terrain is mostly moderate, which makes it a good introduction to Dolomites touring, though some peaks are steep and rocky.
fanes.beyond: The rifugi serve excellent South Tyrolean and Ladin food, and Lavarella brews its own beer. The area is full of Ladin legends about the lost Kingdom of Fanes, and the famous Lago di Braies is on the edge of the park.
fanes.know:
Access is from San Vigilio di Marebbe and the Pederü hut, with snowcat taxis to some rifugi. Rifugi open in winter and spring; book ahead. Venice and Innsbruck are about 2.5 hours away.

The Dolomites' snowpack is often thin and weak: check the South Tyrol avalanche bulletin carefully.

julianalps.skiing:
Slovenia's Julian Alps catch heavy snowfall from the Adriatic and offer limestone karst terrain unlike anywhere else in the Alps: bowls, sinkholes and steep gullies. **Kanin**, above Bovec, is the highest ski area in Slovenia and links to Sella Nevea in Italy, giving access to touring and freeride terrain. Its lifts have had long closures in recent years, so check before you go.

Triglav (2,864 m), Slovenia's highest peak and a national symbol on its flag, is a more serious objective. Vogel, above Lake Bohinj, is a small ski area with one of the best lake views in the Alps.
julianalps.beyond: The Soča valley is famous for its emerald river. Kobarid has an excellent museum about the First World War front on the Soča, the setting for Hemingway's *A Farewell to Arms*. Planica, near Kranjska Gora, has the world's biggest ski-flying hill. Ljubljana and Lake Bled are close for days off.
julianalps.know:
Many mountain huts are closed in winter, so tours are often day trips from the valley. Ljubljana is about 2 hours away; Trieste and Venice are close too. The Vršič pass is closed in winter.

The karst terrain hides holes and drops, so go with a local guide. Slovenia's avalanche bulletin is published by ARSO.

whistler.skiing:
Two big mountains, Whistler and Blackcomb, linked at the top by the Peak 2 Peak gondola, make this the largest ski area in North America, with more than 200 marked runs and about 1,600 m of vertical. Above the trees are wide alpine bowls and glaciers; below them, long groomers and good tree skiing for storm days.

The coastal location brings lots of snow, but also mild storms: it can be rain at the village while it dumps up top.
whistler.beyond: A busy, pedestrian village with every kind of restaurant, bar and shop. The Sea-to-Sky Highway from Vancouver is one of the most scenic drives anywhere, and Vancouver itself is easy to add to the trip.
whistler.know:
About 2 hours by road from Vancouver airport, with regular shuttle buses. It's busy and expensive, especially at weekends and holidays, when lift lines can be long.

Check the freezing level: when it's high, ski the alpine and avoid the lower runs. Avalanche Canada covers the backcountry; the resort's own terrain is controlled.

mammoth.skiing:
Mammoth Mountain is a dormant volcano rising to about 3,370 m above the Eastern Sierra, and one of the biggest ski areas in California. The terrain covers everything: wide groomers and parks lower down, and a summit ridge of steep chutes and bowls that are open when the wind allows.

Its altitude and big Sierra storms give one of the longest seasons in North America, often running into June and, in big years, to July 4th. Dave McCoy started it with a portable rope tow and grew it into a giant. June Mountain, nearby, is the quieter sister.
mammoth.beyond: The Eastern Sierra is a spectacular road trip: natural hot springs in the desert, the tufa towers of Mono Lake and the basalt columns of Devils Postpile. The town of Mammoth Lakes has plenty of restaurants and breweries.
mammoth.know:
Los Angeles is about 5 to 6 hours by car; flights to the small local airports are limited and change from year to year. Tioga Pass, the shortcut from the Bay Area through Yosemite, is closed in winter. Weekends bring crowds from Southern California.

Wind closes the upper lifts often. The Eastern Sierra Avalanche Center forecasts the backcountry.

cottonwoods.skiing:
Two canyons above Salt Lake City hold four resorts with some of the deepest, driest snow in North America, the basis of Utah's "Greatest Snow on Earth" slogan. In **Little Cottonwood**, **Alta** (skiers only, no snowboards) has legendary traverses and old-school charm, and **Snowbird** has a tram, steep terrain and over 1,000 m of vertical. **Big Cottonwood** has **Brighton** and **Solitude**, smaller, cheaper and more local.

The backcountry between the canyons is famous too, and very busy on powder days.
cottonwoods.beyond: Salt Lake City is a 40-minute drive, so you can stay in town and ski the canyons, or stay at a classic lodge such as the Alta Lodge for the full mountain experience.
cottonwoods.know:
Salt Lake City airport is about 40 minutes away. Little Cottonwood Canyon's road often closes for avalanche control. During "interlodge", guests at the top have to stay indoors until it's safe. Traffic on powder mornings can be severe, so take the bus or start very early.

The Utah Avalanche Center forecasts the backcountry daily.

parkcity.skiing:
Since Canyons and Park City were linked in 2015, Park City Mountain is one of the largest ski areas in the US. It has lots of terrain for every level, with long groomers, bowls and trees. **Deer Valley**, next door, is skiers-only and known for immaculate grooming and service.

The snow is drier than the Cottonwoods, though less deep.
parkcity.beyond: Park City is an old silver-mining town with a lively Main Street of bars, restaurants and galleries. Several events of the 2002 Winter Olympics were held here, and at the Utah Olympic Park you can ride the bobsled track with a pilot. The Sundance Film Festival has made January famous here, though it's moving to Boulder from 2027.
parkcity.know:
Salt Lake City airport is about 40 minutes away. Free buses run around town, so you don't need a car. Holidays and weekends are busy.

The Utah Avalanche Center covers the backcountry. The Cottonwoods are close for a powder day.

jackson.skiing:
Jackson Hole is America's big-mountain resort: around 1,260 m of continuous vertical, served by the red Aerial Tram to the top of Rendezvous Mountain. **Corbet's Couloir**, a cliff drop into a narrow chute right under the tram, is one of the most famous runs in the world. The rest of the mountain is steep, with chutes, cliffs and big bowls.

The resort has backcountry gates, and the terrain beyond them is huge and serious.
jackson.beyond: The town of Jackson is a Western mountain town with good food, galleries and the Million Dollar Cowboy Bar, where the bar stools are saddles. Sleigh rides go through the National Elk Refuge, where thousands of elk spend the winter. Grand Targhee, on the other side of the Tetons, is a quieter, snowier alternative.
jackson.know:
Jackson's airport is inside Grand Teton National Park, with flights from many US hubs. Teton Village is at the base of the resort; the town is about 20 minutes away.

The terrain is steep. If you're new to it, ski with a guide or join a steep-skiing camp. Bridger-Teton Avalanche Center forecasts the backcountry.

bigsky.skiing:
Big Sky is huge and uncrowded, with **Lone Peak** at its centre, a pyramid of a mountain at about 3,400 m. A tram climbs to the summit, and from there steep, exposed terrain drops in every direction. The **Big Couloir** requires a partner and avalanche gear.

Below the peak, the resort has long cruisers, bowls and trees, with rarely a lift line, even on busy days.
bigsky.beyond: Yellowstone National Park is close: snowcoach tours run to Old Faithful in winter, and the wildlife is spectacular. Bozeman has a lively college-town feel, with good restaurants and breweries.
bigsky.know:
Bozeman airport is about 1 hour away, with flights from many US cities. The resort is remote, so most people stay on the mountain or in the small Big Sky town.

The Gallatin National Forest Avalanche Center forecasts the backcountry.

Big Sky is pricier than most of Montana, and lodging on the mountain books up in holiday weeks. Staying in Bozeman and driving up is cheaper, though the canyon road is long and can be icy. Montana's smaller hills, like Bridger Bowl near Bozeman, make a good local day.

aspen.skiing:
Aspen Snowmass is four mountains on one pass. **Aspen Mountain** (Ajax) rises right from town, with steep runs and no beginner terrain. **Aspen Highlands** has the **Highland Bowl**, a hike-to bowl at about 3,780 m with some of the best inbounds steeps in Colorado. **Snowmass** is the big one, with lots of variety; **Buttermilk** is gentle and hosts the X Games.

The snow is dry and Colorado's continental snowpack is often weak.
aspen.beyond: Aspen was a silver-mining town, and after the war, veterans of the 10th Mountain Division helped turn it into a ski resort. Today it's known for luxury and celebrities, but the Victorian town, the Hotel Jerome and the Wheeler Opera House still give it real character.
aspen.know:
Aspen has its own airport, with flights from US hubs; Denver is about 3.5 to 4 hours by car, since Independence Pass is closed in winter. Free buses link the four mountains.

It's expensive, especially in town. The Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts the backcountry.

vail.skiing:
Vail is one of the biggest ski areas in North America. The front side is classic groomed skiing; behind it, the **Back Bowls** stretch for kilometres, wide open and treeless. Further back, **Blue Sky Basin** has more remote-feeling terrain with gladed trees.

Vail was founded in 1962 by veterans of the 10th Mountain Division, who trained in the nearby mountains during the Second World War. Beaver Creek, nearby, hosts the Birds of Prey World Cup races.
vail.beyond: The village is built in a Bavarian style, with pedestrian streets, restaurants and shops. Beaver Creek is more upscale and calm. Both are expensive.
vail.know:
Eagle County airport is about 40 minutes away; Denver is about 2 hours, but I-70 traffic on weekends can make it much longer.

The Colorado snowpack is often weak, so be careful in the backcountry. The Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts daily.

Vail is on the Epic Pass, and buying a pass ahead is far cheaper than walk-up tickets, which are among the most expensive in the world. Staying in Avon, Edwards or Minturn is cheaper than the village, with free buses.

summit.skiing:
Summit County is a cluster of resorts within an hour or two of Denver. **Breckenridge** has the Imperial Express, one of the highest chairlifts in North America. **Keystone** has night skiing; **Copper Mountain** separates its terrain neatly by difficulty. **Arapahoe Basin** is high, steep and old-school, often open into June; **Loveland** sits right on the Continental Divide.

Everything is high, with bases at around 2,900 m, so the snow is dry and the season long.
summit.beyond: Breckenridge is an old mining town with a pretty Victorian main street. At A-Basin, the parking lot by the slopes, known as "the Beach", is famous for spring tailgating.
summit.know:
Denver airport is about 2 hours away, but I-70 traffic on weekends can be very slow. The resorts are on different passes (Epic and Ikon), so check which one you need.

The altitude is high: drink lots of water and take it easy the first day. The Colorado snowpack is weak; check the CAIC forecast.

steamboat.skiing:
Steamboat is known for its tree skiing and for "Champagne Powder", a name it trademarked for its light, dry snow. Aspen glades and open terrain cover a big mountain, and the resort is good for everyone, from families to tree skiers.

Howelsen Hill, in town, is one of the oldest ski areas in the US, operating since 1915, and has produced many Olympians.
steamboat.beyond:
Steamboat is a real ranching town with a Western feel, rather than a purpose-built resort. Strawberry Park Hot Springs, in the hills above town, is a beautiful place to soak in the snow.

The town has produced more Winter Olympians than almost any other in the US, earning it the nickname "Ski Town USA". Cowboys in the lift line are not a costume: ranching is still part of daily life in the Yampa Valley.
steamboat.know:
Yampa Valley airport, at Hayden, is about 30 minutes away, with seasonal direct flights. Denver is about 3 hours by car.

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center covers the backcountry.

telluride.skiing:
Telluride is a former mining town in a box canyon in the San Juan Mountains, with a ski area rising right behind it. The terrain is big and varied: groomers for all levels, plus hike-to steeps on Palmyra Peak and the chutes of Gold Hill, among the best expert terrain in Colorado.

It's remote, so even on busy days the lift lines are short.
telluride.beyond: The town is a National Historic Landmark, with Victorian buildings and a main street that feels untouched by mass tourism. Butch Cassidy robbed his first bank here in 1889. A free gondola links the town to Mountain Village, running until late in the evening.
telluride.know:
Montrose airport is about 1.5 hours away; the small Telluride airport is often affected by weather. Denver is about 6 hours by car.

The San Juans have one of the weakest snowpacks in North America; check the Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecast carefully before going out of bounds.

crestedbutte.skiing:
Crested Butte is famous for its "Extreme Limits", steep, rocky inbounds terrain that hosted some of the first extreme skiing competitions in the US. Below the steeps, the mountain has good intermediate runs and a relaxed, uncrowded feel.

It's often called the last great Colorado ski town, because it's so remote and still feels like a small community.

Crested Butte is quiet midweek, and on a powder day the locals know which steep zones open first. It's a mountain that rewards a few days to learn its secrets, rather than a single visit.
crestedbutte.beyond: The town of Crested Butte, an old coal-mining town, has a colourful main street (Elk Avenue) with good restaurants and bars. Cross-country skiing and fat biking are popular.
crestedbutte.know:
Gunnison airport is about 45 minutes away. Denver is about 4.5 hours by car.

The snowpack is often weak; the Crested Butte Avalanche Center forecasts the backcountry.

taos.skiing:
Taos Ski Valley, founded by Ernie Blake in 1955, has some of the steepest inbounds terrain in North America. The **Kachina Peak** lift, added in 2014, reaches about 3,800 m, and the **Highline Ridge** is a hike for steep chutes.

The resort has a European feel, with a small village at the base and ski school traditions. Snowboarding has been allowed since 2008.
taos.beyond: Taos is a fascinating town with adobe buildings, art galleries and New Mexican food. Order your chile "Christmas" (red and green). Taos Pueblo, a UNESCO site, has been lived in for about 1,000 years.
taos.know:
Albuquerque is about 2.5 hours away; Santa Fe is about 1.5 hours. The altitude is high, so take it easy at first.

The snowpack in New Mexico is often thin and weak; check the Taos Avalanche Center forecast.

Taos Ski Valley is a small, high village at the end of a winding canyon road. Staying in the valley gives you the full experience; staying in the town of Taos gives you more food and culture, about 30 minutes away.

sunvalley.skiing:
Sun Valley was America's first destination ski resort, built in 1936 by the Union Pacific railroad, and it's where the world's first chairlifts were installed. **Bald Mountain** (Baldy) has about 1,000 m of steady, consistent fall-line vertical, with very little flat terrain and excellent grooming. **Dollar Mountain** is the gentle beginner's hill.

The snow is often thin by Western standards, but snowmaking is strong and the skiing is smooth and fast.

Baldy has some of the best grooming in the world and few lift lines, which makes it a dream for skiers who love speed and carving. It's less of a powder mountain, but the bowls on the back side can be excellent after a storm.
sunvalley.beyond: Sun Valley has a long Hollywood history, and the Sun Valley Lodge still has the old-school glamour. Ernest Hemingway lived in nearby Ketchum and is buried there. The town has excellent restaurants and a relaxed feel.
sunvalley.know:
Friedman Memorial airport, in Hailey, is about 20 minutes away, but flights are limited and weather can divert them to Twin Falls or Boise.

The Sawtooth Avalanche Center forecasts the backcountry.

mtbaker.skiing:
Mt. Baker Ski Area holds the world record for snowfall in a single season: about 29 m in 1998–99. The terrain is steep and varied, with natural halfpipes, cliffs and trees, and the views of Mount Shuksan are some of the most dramatic in North America.

There's no lodging at the mountain, no village and no real resort scene. It's all about the snow and the terrain, and the backcountry beyond the gates is excellent.
mtbaker.beyond: The Legendary Baker Banked Slalom, held each February since 1985, is one of the most loved events in snowboarding. The small town of Glacier, at the bottom of the road, has a couple of places to eat and stay; Bellingham is a pleasant college town.
mtbaker.know:
Bellingham is about 1.5 hours away; Seattle is about 2.5 hours. The road up is winding and snowy.

The Pacific snowpack is heavy and wet. Storm slabs and tree wells are common. The Northwest Avalanche Center forecasts the area.

silverton.skiing:
Silverton Mountain is unlike any other US ski area: a single old chairlift serving steep, ungroomed, avalanche-controlled terrain at high altitude. For much of the season, skiing is guided only, in small groups, and the hikes from the top of the lift open even more terrain. Heli drops are available too.

It's expert-only, with no groomed runs or easy way down.
silverton.beyond: Silverton is a former mining town with a Wild West feel, high in the San Juans. In summer, the Durango & Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad steams up the canyon. Ouray, over the pass, has hot springs and a famous ice-climbing park.
silverton.know:
Durango is about 1.5 hours away by road, over high mountain passes that can close in storms. Book guided days ahead.

The San Juans have one of the weakest snowpacks in North America; listen to your guide. The Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts daily.

The town is small, with a handful of hotels, cafés and bars, many open only in season. Pack layers: the base area sits above 3,200 m and the top is much higher, so the cold and altitude can hit hard.

revelstoke.skiing:
Revelstoke Mountain Resort has the biggest lift-served vertical in North America, about 1,710 m, from the top of Mount Mackenzie to the town's edge. The snow is deep and frequent, and the terrain is steep, with old-growth trees, open bowls and long runs that test your legs.

Revelstoke is also a hub for heli-skiing, cat skiing and backcountry touring, with Rogers Pass close by.
revelstoke.beyond: The town of Revelstoke is a real railway town with a historic downtown, good restaurants and breweries. The Railway Museum tells the story of the transcontinental railway through the mountains.
revelstoke.know:
Kelowna airport is about 2.5 to 3 hours away; Calgary is about 5 hours. The roads can be difficult in winter.

Interior BC's snowpack often has buried weak layers. Avalanche Canada forecasts daily.

The resort also has easier terrain, but the mountain is at its best for strong skiers. Stay in town rather than at the base for the restaurants and better value; the gondola is a short drive away. Cat-skiing and heli operators run day trips from town.

kickinghorse.skiing:
Kicking Horse, above the town of Golden, is a steep, serious mountain with over 100 chutes and about 1,260 m of vertical from one gondola. The terrain includes big open bowls, rocky ridges and steep chutes, with fewer easy runs than most resorts.

It's a favourite of freeriders who like to work for their turns.
kickinghorse.beyond: The Eagle's Eye restaurant, at the top of the gondola, is the highest restaurant in Canada. Golden is a working town on the railway and the Trans-Canada Highway, with a long timber-frame pedestrian bridge over the Kicking Horse River.
kickinghorse.know:
Calgary airport is about 3 hours away by road, through Banff and Yoho national parks. The Trans-Canada Highway can close in storms.

The terrain is steep and avalanche-prone off-piste. Avalanche Canada forecasts daily.

Golden is a good base for a road trip: Revelstoke, Rogers Pass and Lake Louise are all within about 1.5 hours. Stay in town for more food choices, or at the base for ski-in access.

fernie.skiing:
Fernie Alpine Resort has five big bowls (Cedar, Lizard, Currie, Timber and Siberia) that catch deep snow from storms coming over the Rockies. The terrain is varied, with open bowls, steep chutes and good tree skiing.

It's one of the best powder resorts in the Canadian Rockies.
fernie.beyond: Fernie is an old coal-mining town with a pretty historic centre, good bars and a local brewery. Locals celebrate the "Legend of the Griz", a mythical mountain man who brings the snow, each winter. Island Lake Lodge, nearby, runs famous cat-skiing trips.
fernie.know:
Cranbrook airport is about 1 hour away; Calgary is about 3 hours. Rain at the base is possible in warm spells.

The snowpack can have buried weak layers. Avalanche Canada forecasts daily.

Fernie can be combined with Kimberley and Panorama on a road trip through the Rockies. Lodging ranges from slopeside condos to cheaper motels and hostels in town, about 10 minutes away.

kootenays.skiing:
Two small, deep-snow resorts in the West Kootenays: **Whitewater**, above Nelson, and **RED Mountain**, above Rossland. Whitewater has steep bowls and trees, and is famous for its food. RED has steep tree skiing on several peaks, including Grey Mountain, added in 2013.

Both are uncrowded, local and full of character, and the area is the heart of BC's "Powder Highway".
kootenays.beyond: Nelson is a colourful heritage town, known for its arts and counterculture, and the setting for the film *Roxanne*. Rossland is a gold-mining town that hosted the first ski races in Canada in the 1890s.
kootenays.know:
Castlegar is the nearest airport, nicknamed "Cancelgar" because flights are often cancelled by weather. Spokane, in the US, is about 2.5 to 3 hours away.

The snowpack often has buried weak layers. Avalanche Canada forecasts daily.

The two resorts are about 1 hour apart, so a week can easily combine both. Cat-skiing operators around Nelson and Rossland offer excellent days, and Kootenay Pass on Highway 3 is a popular backcountry spot.

banff.skiing:
Banff National Park has three resorts on one pass (SkiBig3): **Lake Louise**, big, varied and scenic, with back bowls; **Sunshine Village**, high and snowy, with the Delirium Dive, where avalanche gear is required; and **Mt Norquay**, small, steep and close to town.

The terrain is big and spectacular, and the season long.
banff.beyond: The town of Banff sits inside a national park, with elk wandering through it. The Banff Upper Hot Springs and the Fairmont Banff Springs hotel are classics, and skating on the frozen Lake Louise is magical.
banff.know:
Calgary airport is about 1.5 hours away. January can be bitterly cold, sometimes below −25 °C.

The Rockies' snowpack is often thin and weak. Avalanche Canada and Parks Canada forecast daily.

The three resorts are spread out, so a car or the SkiBig3 shuttle buses are needed. Staying in Banff gives you restaurants and nightlife; Lake Louise village is quieter. Book the shuttle or plan parking for weekends, when Calgary skiers arrive.

bigwhite.skiing:
Big White, near Kelowna, is known for its light Okanagan powder and its "snow ghosts": trees coated in rime ice near the top. The terrain is mostly intermediate, with good tree skiing and some steeper runs.

The village is the biggest ski-in, ski-out village in Canada, and very family-friendly.
bigwhite.beyond: The Okanagan Valley is wine country, and Kelowna has good restaurants and wineries. The resort is very popular with Australians, many of whom work there for the season.
bigwhite.know:
Kelowna airport is about 1 hour away. The top of the mountain is often in cloud, earning it the nickname "Big White-out".

Avalanche Canada forecasts the backcountry.

Everything is in the village, so most people stay a week without a car. Night skiing runs several evenings a week, and the tube park and ice-skating rink keep kids busy. Silver Star and Apex, nearby, are good day trips.

wolfcreek.skiing:
Wolf Creek gets the most snow in Colorado, on average more than 10 m a year, thanks to its spot on the Continental Divide. It's a family-owned ski area with no village and no lodging at the base, just good terrain and deep snow.

The Alberta Peak and the Knife Ridge offer hike-to steeps, and the resort often opens early in the season.
wolfcreek.beyond: Pagosa Springs, about 30 minutes away, has hot springs, including the Mother Spring, one of the deepest geothermal springs in the world. Durango is a lively college town.
wolfcreek.know:
Durango airport is about 1.5 hours away. Wolf Creek Pass can close in storms. Lift tickets are good value.

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts the area.

There's no lodging at the ski area, so most people stay in Pagosa Springs or South Fork. Wolf Creek's season often starts in early November and runs into April, longer than many Colorado resorts.

winterpark.skiing:
Winter Park is the closest big resort to Denver and is owned by the city. **Mary Jane**, its sister mountain, is famous for steep bumps. The resort has lots of variety, with tree skiing, bowls and long groomers.

The Winter Park Express ski train runs from Denver's Union Station, one of the only ski trains in the US.
winterpark.beyond: The town of Fraser, nearby, calls itself the "Icebox of the Nation" for its cold winters. The area has good cross-country skiing and snowmobiling.
winterpark.know:
Denver is about 1.5 to 2 hours away by car, over Berthoud Pass. The ski train runs on weekends in season.

The Colorado snowpack is weak. The Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts daily.

Winter Park is a good choice for a short trip from Denver, and it's popular with locals on weekends. Staying in the base village or in Fraser avoids the drive. The resort is on the Ikon Pass.

ogden.skiing:
Two very different resorts near Ogden. **Snowbasin** hosted the downhill races at the 2002 Winter Olympics, and has grand day lodges and long, fast runs. **Powder Mountain** is huge and uncrowded, with lots of tree skiing, open terrain and cat skiing on Lightning Ridge.

Together they offer a quieter alternative to the Cottonwoods and Park City.
ogden.beyond: Ogden was a railway town, and its historic 25th Street has good bars and restaurants. Salt Lake City is about 1 hour away.
ogden.know:
Salt Lake City airport is about 1 hour away. Powder Mountain has its own rules about tickets and access, so check before you go.

The Utah Avalanche Center forecasts the backcountry.

Ogden is less crowded than Salt Lake's canyons, with cheaper lodging in town. Both resorts are about 30 to 45 minutes from downtown Ogden. Nordic Valley, a small local hill, offers night skiing.

rogerspass.skiing:
Rogers Pass, in Glacier National Park, is the most famous road-accessed backcountry in Canada. The Trans-Canada Highway crosses the Selkirks here, right through some of the heaviest snowfall in the country: steep old-growth trees on storm days, and on clear days big alpine terrain and glaciers around peaks like Sir Donald, whose pointed summit dominates the pass.

There are no lifts. Areas like the Asulkan valley, Balu Pass and the Illecillewaet glacier offer everything from short tree laps to long glacier days, and the Alpine Club of Canada's huts allow multi-day trips.
rogerspass.beyond: The pass has a dramatic history. The railway crossed it in the 1880s, and in 1910 an avalanche killed 58 railway workers clearing an earlier slide; the railway then tunnelled under the pass. Today the Canadian army fires artillery to bring down avalanches above the highway. The Discovery Centre tells the story. Revelstoke and Golden are the nearest towns.
rogerspass.know:
You need a free winter permit from Parks Canada, and areas are open or closed day by day depending on avalanche control. Check the daily status before setting out, and never enter a closed area.

Avalanche Canada forecasts specifically for Glacier National Park. Huts need booking.

bcheli.skiing:
Heli-skiing was born in the Interior of British Columbia: Hans Gmoser flew his first guests into the Bugaboos in the 1960s, and the company he founded, CMH, still runs lodges across the region. Today, operators in the Selkirks, Monashees, Purcells and Cariboos fly skiers into old-growth trees on storm days and onto alpine glaciers when it clears.

The snow is deep and frequent, and a week can bring an enormous amount of vertical. Cat skiing offers similar terrain, often in the trees, at a lower price.
bcheli.beyond: Lodges range from comfortable to luxurious, with food, saunas and massage included. Many are reached only by helicopter, and the evenings, with fellow guests swapping stories, are part of the experience.
bcheli.know:
This is among the most expensive skiing in the world, and popular weeks book up a year or more ahead. Most operators sell trips by the week, with day trips and cat skiing as cheaper ways in.

Operators run professional avalanche programs, but weather can ground helicopters for days. Strong powder skiing and good fitness help you get the most out of it.

tetonpass.skiing:
Teton Pass, on the road between Jackson and Idaho, is one of the most popular road-accessed backcountry areas in the US. From the top of the pass, tours go in every direction, from mellow tree laps to big, steep descents like Glory Bowl, a famous slide path above the highway.

In spring, Grand Teton National Park offers serious ski mountaineering. The Grand Teton itself was first skied in 1971, and its big couloirs are classics for experienced ski mountaineers.
tetonpass.beyond: Jackson is close, with good food and a Western feel. Jackson Hole and Grand Targhee are nearby for lift-served days. On the Idaho side, Victor and Driggs are quieter, cheaper bases.
tetonpass.know:
The parking at the top of the pass fills early. Respect the road: slides can reach it, so never trigger slopes above the highway, and follow local etiquette.

The Bridger-Teton Avalanche Center forecasts daily, and the snowpack often has persistent weak layers. Local guides and avalanche courses are easy to find in Jackson.

tenthmountain.skiing:
The 10th Mountain Division Hut Association runs a network of around 30 backcountry huts in the Colorado Rockies between Vail, Aspen and Leadville. It's named after the army's mountain troops, who trained at Camp Hale nearby during the Second World War and later helped found Colorado's ski industry. Several huts honour soldiers who died in the war.

Most of the touring is moderate: long approaches through forest to huts at around 3,300 m, with good tree skiing nearby. It's more about the hut experience than big descents.
tenthmountain.beyond: The huts are cosy, with wood stoves, bunks and kitchens. You bring your own food and sleeping bag. Evenings with friends in a hut far from any road are the highlight. Camp Hale is now a national monument.
tenthmountain.know:
Popular dates book up fast, with a booking lottery for peak dates. The altitude is high, so acclimatise first. Navigation can be challenging in storms.

The Colorado snowpack is weak; the Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts daily.

sanjuans.skiing:
Road-accessed touring around Red Mountain Pass, between Silverton and Ouray, in the high San Juan Mountains. The terrain is big and alpine, with steep slopes above old mines and avalanche paths that cross the highway. Huts and old mining buildings allow multi-day trips.

The San Juans have one of the weakest snowpacks in North America, so conservative decisions are essential.
sanjuans.beyond:
Ouray has natural hot springs and a famous ice-climbing park. Silverton is a historic mining town, and its avalanche school is one of the oldest in the US. Both towns are small and full of character.

The old mines and ghost towns scattered across the mountains give the area a haunted, historic feel, and many hut trips use restored mining buildings.
sanjuans.know:
The pass road, known as the Million Dollar Highway, is steep, narrow and can close in storms. Silverton and Ouray are the bases; Durango and Montrose have the nearest airports.

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts daily. Going with a local guide is a good idea, especially early in the season.

cascadevolcanoes.skiing:
A spring road trip to ski the big Cascade volcanoes: Hood, Adams, St. Helens, Rainier and Baker. Each offers a long climb on skins and crampons, then a descent of around 1,500 to 2,000 m on corn snow, with views of the other volcanoes lined up along the horizon.

St. Helens lets you ski from the rim of the crater left by the 1980 eruption. The higher peaks, like Rainier and Baker, are glaciated, with crevasses and serious mountaineering hazards.
cascadevolcanoes.beyond: Timberline Lodge on Mount Hood, built in the 1930s, is a classic, and you may recognise it from *The Shining*. The Pacific Northwest also offers great food, coffee and breweries in Portland and Seattle, and lots of camping and hot springs along the way.
cascadevolcanoes.know:
The best season is roughly May to July. Climbing permits are required on several peaks, including Rainier and St. Helens.

Glacier travel skills are essential on the higher peaks. Start early, before the snow softens too much. The Northwest Avalanche Center covers the area.

easternsierra.skiing:
Huge couloirs and open faces rise straight above Highway 395 between Bishop, Mammoth and Lone Pine, with some of the biggest vertical from the road in the lower 48. In spring, the Eastern Sierra is one of the best places in the world for corn snow on big, steep lines, and peaks like Mount Tom tower above the desert.

Midwinter brings big storms and powder, but spring is the classic season. When the Tioga Pass road opens in late spring, it gives access to more high terrain.
easternsierra.beyond: Natural hot springs, desert landscapes and the small towns of Bishop and Lone Pine make it a great road trip. The Alabama Hills, near Lone Pine, have been the backdrop for many westerns. Death Valley and Yosemite are within reach.
easternsierra.know:
The season runs roughly from January to June, with the best corn in March to May. Some peaks, like Mount Whitney, need permits.

The Eastern Sierra Avalanche Center forecasts the area. Long approaches and big vertical mean early starts.

wapta.skiing:
The Wapta Icefield traverse is the Canadian Rockies' classic hut-to-hut glacier trip, off the Icefields Parkway. It links the Bow, Peyto, Balfour and Scott Duncan huts across glaciers and passes over about four to six days, with optional summits like Mount Gordon and Mount Olive along the way.

The terrain is glaciated and high, with crevasses and exposure to weather.
wapta.beyond: The Icefields Parkway is one of the most scenic roads in the world. Num-Ti-Jah Lodge, at Bow Lake, has a long history in the Rockies. Lake Louise and Banff are close for a rest day.
wapta.know:
The main season is roughly March to May. Huts are run by the Alpine Club of Canada, are self-catered and need booking.

Glacier travel skills and good navigation are essential, or go with a guide. The Rockies' snowpack often has weak layers; Avalanche Canada forecasts daily.

Most parties start at Bow Lake and finish on the Yoho side, so plan a car shuttle. The ACC huts have stoves, pots and foam mattresses, so you need only food and a sleeping bag.

sierrahr.skiing:
