A committing multi-day ski traverse across the high Sierra Nevada, from the Eastern Sierra near Mount Whitney to Sequoia National Park, through wilderness with no huts for most of the way. It crosses high passes and alpine basins over about six to seven days, among some of the wildest terrain in the lower 48.

You carry everything, camp in the snow and need strong navigation and skiing skills.
sierrahr.beyond: The scenery is spectacular: granite peaks, frozen lakes and giant sequoias on the western side. The Pear Lake Ski Hut in Sequoia is a welcome stop near the end.
sierrahr.know:
Spring (roughly March to May) is the season. A wilderness permit is required. Plan the logistics carefully: the start and finish are far apart by road.

The Eastern Sierra Avalanche Center covers the eastern side. Go with a guide unless you're experienced in multi-day backcountry travel.

A wilderness permit is needed, and quotas may apply. Bear-resistant food storage is required in some areas, even in spring.

shasta.skiing:
Mount Shasta is a lone volcano, about 4,320 m high, rising far above the surrounding country. It offers long corn-snow descents of around 2,000 m on several sides, from the popular Avalanche Gulch to quieter routes on the north side. It's a classic spring and early-summer objective.

The climb is long and the summit high, so altitude and weather matter.
shasta.beyond: The town of Mount Shasta has a quirky, spiritual reputation. The Sierra Club's stone Horse Camp cabin, from the 1920s, sits on the main route. Lassen Volcanic National Park is about 1.5 hours away for more volcano skiing.
shasta.know:
A summit pass and wilderness permit are required, and you must carry out your human waste in bags provided at the trailhead. The best season is roughly May to June.

The Mount Shasta Avalanche Center forecasts the area. Weather on the summit can change very fast.

Many people camp at Horse Camp or Helen Lake to split the climb into two days, which also helps with acclimatisation. Guided climbs are available in town.

bclodges.skiing:
Backcountry lodges in the Selkirks, Purcells and Monashees offer a week of touring from the door. You fly in by helicopter to a timber lodge near treeline, then tour each day on terrain that ranges from tree runs to alpine bowls and glaciers. The Alpine Club of Canada's Fairy Meadow hut, in the Adamants, is one of the most famous.

The Interior BC snowpack is deep, and the skiing is some of the best in the world.
bclodges.beyond:
Lodges are cosy, with saunas and good food. The isolation, far from any road, is a big part of the appeal.

Many lodges have a long history, built by ski pioneers in the 1970s and 1980s. Guests often return to the same lodge year after year, and a week with the same small group of people builds strong friendships.
bclodges.know:
Lodges can be guided or self-guided, and catered or self-catered. Trips usually run Saturday to Saturday, with helicopter flights from towns like Golden, Revelstoke or Nelson. Popular weeks book up a year ahead.

The interior snowpack has buried weak layers; Avalanche Canada forecasts daily.

wapass.skiing:
Each spring, the North Cascades Highway (State Route 20) reopens after winter, giving road access to steep granite couloirs and glaciers around Washington Pass. Peaks like Liberty Bell and the Early Winters Spires tower above the road. The terrain is big, steep and dramatic.

The season is short, usually from the road opening in spring until the snow melts.
wapass.beyond: The Methow Valley has one of the largest cross-country ski networks in North America, and Winthrop has a Western-style main street. Mazama is a small, friendly base for climbers and skiers.
wapass.know:
The highway is closed all winter and usually reopens in spring; check the reopening date before planning. There are no services at the pass.

The Northwest Avalanche Center forecasts the area. Wet slides and cornices are the main spring hazards.

North Cascades Heli, based in Mazama, is the only heli-ski operator in Washington. Lodging in Mazama and Winthrop fills up quickly in spring; book ahead.

gudauri.skiing:
Gudauri sits high on the Georgian Military Highway in the Greater Caucasus, with lifts climbing above 3,000 m over wide, treeless slopes. The pistes are simple and uncrowded, but the draw is the open freeride terrain between and beyond them, plus heli-skiing at prices far below the Alps or Canada.

With no trees, storm days and flat light are hard, and the big open slopes are serious avalanche terrain.
gudauri.beyond: Georgian food and wine are a highlight of any trip: khachapuri, khinkali, and wine made in clay qvevri jars. Kazbegi (Stepantsminda), with the Gergeti Trinity Church under Mount Kazbek, is a short drive further up the highway.
gudauri.know:
Tbilisi is about 2 to 2.5 hours away by road. The highway is the main route to Russia, so expect truck traffic, and the pass above Gudauri can close in storms.

There's no full public avalanche forecast like in the Alps, and off-piste accidents happen every winter: hire a local guide. It's very good value.

svaneti.skiing:
Upper Svaneti sits under the highest peaks of the Caucasus, with mountains of 4,000 to 5,000 m. Two small ski areas near Mestia, Hatsvali and Tetnuldi, give lift access to big terrain, and from them you can tour into wild, rarely skied mountains.

The terrain is big and remote; this is a place for touring with a guide rather than a resort trip.
svaneti.beyond: The medieval stone defensive towers of Svaneti are a UNESCO World Heritage site, and Ushguli, a cluster of tower villages further up the valley, is one of the highest permanently inhabited villages in Europe. Svan food, music and hospitality make the trip.
svaneti.know:
Mestia has a small airport with flights from Tbilisi that depend on the weather; by road it's a long drive from Kutaisi or Zugdidi. Plan extra days.

There's no public avalanche forecast: go with a local guide who knows the snowpack. Facilities are simple, and English is less common than in Tbilisi.

kackar.skiing:
The Kaçkar Mountains, the highest part of Turkey's Pontic Alps, rise steeply from the Black Sea coast and catch its moisture as deep, maritime snow. Heli-skiing here means steep, treeless ridges and long descents into valleys of stone villages and summer pastures, often with the sea glinting on the horizon.

The terrain is big and largely unskied, and operators run small groups from lodges in the valleys.
kackar.beyond: This is the land of the Laz and Hemşin peoples, with their own languages, music and food. Rize, on the coast, is the heart of Turkey's tea country, and tea terraces climb the hillsides. Ayder, a mountain village with hot springs, is a classic stop. Near Trabzon, the Sumela Monastery clings to a cliff face.
kackar.know:
Trabzon is the nearest airport, with flights from Istanbul. Most visitors book a heli-ski week through an operator, which arranges transfers.

The maritime snowpack brings storm slabs and wet slides in spring. Weather can ground the helicopter for days, so allow for down days.

gulmarg.skiing:
Gulmarg's two-stage gondola climbs from a meadow town at about 2,650 m to the Apharwat ridge at nearly 4,000 m, one of the highest lift-served points in the world. Below it lies a huge freeride playground: open bowls up high, long descents through pine and fir forests lower down, and very few people.

There are only a few pistes. Gulmarg is about freeride, and the snow can be superb, though storms are heavy and conditions change fast.
gulmarg.beyond: Gulmarg was a British hill station, and has one of the highest golf courses in the world under the snow. Srinagar, 1.5 hours away, is famous for its houseboats and wooden shikara boats on Dal Lake, and for Kashmiri cooking: try a *wazwan*, a multi-course feast, and *kahwa*, a saffron and almond tea.
gulmarg.know:
Srinagar has flights from Delhi and Mumbai. Kashmir is a sensitive region, with a heavy security presence; check your government's travel advice before booking, and expect checkpoints.

Rescue services are limited and the terrain is avalanche-prone, so ski with a local guide. Costs are low compared with almost anywhere else with this terrain.

karakol.skiing:
Karakol, in the Tian Shan of Kyrgyzstan, has a small ski resort with a few lifts and wide open slopes, and around it a huge range of backcountry. Yurt camps and small guesthouses are bases for touring, and cat-skiing operators take skiers deep into the mountains. The snow is dry and continental, often light and cold.

Nearby, the Jyrgalan valley has developed a community-based touring scene, with marked tours and local guides.
karakol.beyond: Lake Issyk-Kul, one of the largest mountain lakes in the world, never freezes. Karakol itself has a wooden Russian Orthodox cathedral and a Chinese-style wooden mosque built by the Dungan community. Try *ashlyan-fu*, the local cold noodle soup. Hot springs at Altyn-Arashan make a good rest day.
karakol.know:
Bishkek is about 6 hours away by road. Infrastructure is simple and prices are low. Pack for real cold.

The continental snowpack is often weak, with persistent layers. There's no public avalanche forecast, so go with a local guide or operator.

iranresorts.skiing:
Iran's Alborz Mountains rise just north of Tehran, and their resorts sit high, at around 2,500 to 3,600 m, with dry, light snow. **Dizin**, opened in 1969, is big and open, with long descents. **Shemshak** is steep and known for moguls. **Tochal**, reached by a long gondola from the northern edge of Tehran, has some of the highest pistes in the region.

The resorts are popular with locals, and weekends (Thursday and Friday) are busy.
iranresorts.beyond: Tehran has excellent museums, the Grand Bazaar and the Golestan Palace. Persian food is a highlight: kebabs, saffron rice, stews and fresh bread. The Chalus road, north over the Alborz to the Caspian, is one of Iran's most scenic drives.
iranresorts.know:
Check your government's travel advice carefully before planning a trip. A visa is required for most nationalities, and international bank cards don't work because of sanctions, so bring cash. Local laws on dress and behaviour apply on the slopes as elsewhere.

Tehran's airport is about 2 to 3 hours from the resorts. Off-piste is uncontrolled; ski with a local guide.

damavand.skiing:
Mount Damavand, at 5,610 m, is the highest volcano in Asia and a near-perfect cone rising above the Alborz. In spring, it offers a huge descent from the summit, where sulphur fumes rise from the crater, down broad slopes to the Bargah-e Sevom hut at about 4,150 m and beyond.

The skiing itself isn't steep. The challenge is the altitude, the wind and the cold near the top.
damavand.beyond: Damavand is central to Persian mythology: in the *Shahnameh*, the national epic, a tyrant is chained inside the mountain. The village of Polour, at the foot, is the gathering point for climbers, and Tehran is a few hours away.
damavand.know:
Check your government's travel advice before planning a trip. Climbers register and pay a fee at the Iranian Mountaineering Federation camp in Polour. Mules can carry gear to the hut.

Spring (roughly May and June) is the season. Acclimatise properly, ideally on nearby peaks first. There's no avalanche forecast.

lebanon.skiing:
Lebanon is one of the few places where you can ski in the morning and swim in the Mediterranean in the afternoon. **Mzaar Kfardebian**, about an hour from Beirut, is the largest resort, with wide open slopes up to about 2,465 m. **The Cedars**, in the north, is smaller and higher, above a grove of ancient cedar trees.

The snow can be excellent after storms but varies a lot from year to year.
lebanon.beyond: The Cedars of God, a grove of ancient trees in the Qadisha valley, is a UNESCO World Heritage site. Lebanese food is one of the great cuisines of the world, from mezze to grilled fish, and Byblos and Batroun are beautiful coastal towns. Beirut has a lively restaurant and nightlife scene.
lebanon.know:
Beirut's airport is about 1 to 2 hours from the resorts. Check your government's travel advice before planning a trip, since the security situation can change quickly.

Weekends are busy with Beirut skiers. Off-piste is uncontrolled.

almaty.skiing:
Almaty is a big, green city at the foot of the Tian Shan, and its ski resort, **Shymbulak**, is reached by a gondola from Medeu, just above town. The lifts climb to the Talgar pass at about 3,200 m, with freeride terrain off both sides and a wall of 4,000 m peaks behind.

It's lift-served freeride with a city at the bottom, and prices are low.
almaty.beyond: Medeu, at the gondola base, is a huge outdoor ice rink where many Soviet speed-skating records were set. Almaty means "father of apples": wild apple forests here are the ancestors of the apples we eat today. The Green Bazaar is the place to try Kazakh food like *beshbarmak* and horse-meat sausage.
almaty.know:
Almaty's international airport is about 45 minutes from the gondola. Many nationalities can visit Kazakhstan without a visa.

The continental snowpack can be weak. Kazakhstan has a local avalanche service, but information in English is limited, so go with a local guide off-piste.

almatytouring.skiing:
Above Almaty, the Trans-Ili Alatau range offers multi-day touring from yurts, mountain huts and old Soviet scientific stations. The Bogdanovich and Tuyuksu glaciers, above Shymbulak, give high, glaciated terrain; the Tuyuksu glacier is one of the most closely studied in the world. Further east, the Turgen gorge and the Ketmen ridge are wilder and quieter.

The terrain ranges from gentle glaciers to big, steep faces.
almatytouring.beyond: The Tien Shan Astronomical Observatory, near the Big Almaty Lake, is an old Soviet observatory that now hosts visitors. The turquoise Big Almaty Lake is beautiful even in winter. Almaty is close for city days.
almatytouring.know:
Almaty's airport is 1 to 2 hours from the trailheads. Local guides and operators arrange yurts, huts and transport.

The snowpack is continental and often weak, and there's limited avalanche information in English. Go with a local guide.

Trips usually last a few days to a week, with yurts or huts as bases. Operators can arrange everything, from guides to transport.

mera.skiing:
Mera Peak (6,476 m) is the classic Himalayan ski objective: a broad, gentle glacier that allows a ski descent from near the summit. From the top, on a clear day, you can see five of the world's 8,000 m peaks, including Everest, Lhotse, Makalu, Cho Oyu and Kangchenjunga.

The skiing isn't technical, but the altitude makes every turn hard work.

The descent is long and gentle, down the glacier from the summit, with some of the best views in the Himalaya. Most skiers are on expeditions with guides and porters.
mera.beyond: The trek in, through the remote Hinku valley, passes forests, Sherpa villages and teahouses. The journey and the people are as memorable as the summit.
mera.know:
Fly from Kathmandu to Lukla; flights are often delayed by weather. A climbing permit is required. Most trips take about two to three weeks, including acclimatisation.

Spring (April to May) has the best snow for skiing. Altitude sickness is the main risk. Crevasses exist on the glacier, so rope up.

annapurna.skiing:
The Annapurna Sanctuary is a high glacial basin surrounded by a ring of 7,000 and 8,000 m peaks, including Annapurna I, the first 8,000 m peak ever climbed, in 1950. Ski touring from the lodges at Annapurna Base Camp (about 4,130 m) means slopes and moraines in one of the most dramatic settings in the world.

The skiing is modest; the setting is extraordinary.
annapurna.beyond: Machapuchare, the "Fishtail" peak, is sacred and closed to climbers. Pokhara, at the start of the trek, is a relaxed lakeside town with views of the Annapurna range. The trek passes Gurung villages and rhododendron forests.
annapurna.know:
The trek in takes several days from near Pokhara. Permits are required for the Annapurna Conservation Area.

The approach trail crosses avalanche paths in the narrow valley below the sanctuary, which can be deadly after heavy snow. Check local conditions and go with an experienced guide.

muztagh.skiing:
Muztagh Ata (7,546 m), the "father of ice mountains", is a huge, rounded peak in the Chinese Pamirs and the classic first 7,000 m peak to ski. Its broad glacier allows a ski descent from near the summit, making it one of the highest ski descents that isn't technically extreme.

The skiing is gentle, but the altitude and cold are serious.
muztagh.beyond: Karakul Lake, at the foot of the mountain, reflects the peak on calm days. Kyrgyz herders live in the area. Kashgar, at the start of the trip, is an ancient Silk Road city with a famous Sunday livestock market.
muztagh.know:
Kashgar is the nearest airport. Travel in Xinjiang involves heavy security, checkpoints and special permits, so go with an experienced expedition operator.

Summer (June to August) is the season. Acclimatise slowly. Crevasses exist on the glacier.

Expeditions usually take about three weeks, including acclimatisation. Operators arrange permits, base camp and logistics.

ararat.skiing:
Mount Ararat (5,137 m), a huge volcano in eastern Türkiye, rises alone from the plain near the borders of Iran and Armenia. In spring, it offers a long ski descent from the snow-capped summit down open slopes.

The skiing isn't steep, but the altitude and weather are challenging.

Ararat is a big, isolated mountain, and the snow can be windblown and icy near the top. The descent is long, with views across the plain into Iran and Armenia, and the scale is enormous.
ararat.beyond: Ararat is said to be where Noah's Ark came to rest, and it's a national symbol of Armenia, visible across the border from Yerevan. Doğubayazıt, at the foot, has the spectacular İshak Pasha Palace on a hillside.
ararat.know:
Climbing Ararat requires a permit from the Turkish authorities, arranged through a licensed agency. Mules carry gear to the camps.

Spring (roughly April to May) is the season. Acclimatise properly. There's no avalanche forecast.

Trips usually take about a week, including acclimatisation on the mountain. Operators in Doğubayazıt arrange permits, mules and guides.

altay.skiing:
The Altay region, in the far north of Xinjiang, has bone-dry powder in rolling hills and forests, and claims to be one of the places where skiing was born. The resort near Hemu, a village of wooden houses, has new lifts and wide open terrain, with long tree runs.

The snow is very cold and light, and the season long.
altay.beyond: Hemu is home to Tuvan and Kazakh communities, who still make traditional skis covered with horse hide. Rock paintings in the Altay are said to show ancient skiers. Kanas Lake, nearby, is famous for its scenery.
altay.know:
Kanas and Altay have small airports with flights from Urumqi. Travel in Xinjiang involves heavy security and permits, so go with an operator.

Midwinter can be extremely cold, below −30 °C. There's no avalanche forecast in English.

Trips are usually arranged through operators that handle permits, transport and lodging in Hemu. The resort is new and growing quickly.

erciyes.skiing:
Erciyes is an extinct volcano (3,917 m) rising above Kayseri, in central Türkiye. The resort has modern lifts and wide, open slopes, mostly above the treeline, with good off-piste on the volcano's flanks.

The snow is often dry, and the views across the plain are huge.

The resort was rebuilt in the 2010s with modern lifts, and the volcano's flanks make for long, varied runs, from wide cruisers to open bowls. After storms, the treeless slopes are an excellent freeride playground, though the wind can quickly strip and pack the snow.
erciyes.beyond: Cappadocia, about an hour away, is famous for its fairy chimneys, cave hotels, underground cities and hot-air balloons at sunrise. Kayseri is known for *pastırma* (cured beef) and *mantı* (dumplings).
erciyes.know:
Kayseri airport is about 30 minutes away, with flights from Istanbul. Prices are low by European standards.

Wind can close the upper lifts. Off-piste is uncontrolled.

Combine a few ski days with a few days in Cappadocia: the cave hotels are about an hour from the slopes, and the dawn balloon flights over the valleys are worth the early start.

uzbekistan.skiing:
Uzbekistan's ski areas sit in the western Tian Shan, about 90 minutes from Tashkent. **Amirsoy**, opened in 2019, has modern lifts and pistes. **Chimgan** and **Beldersay** are older, Soviet-era areas with simple lifts and character. Heli-skiing operates in the surrounding mountains.

The snow can be good, but varies from year to year.

Amirsoy is the modern side, with gondolas, groomed runs and a resort hotel. Chimgan is the old-school side, with Soviet lifts, quirky charm and steeper terrain. Heli-skiing in the Chimgan and Ugam ranges offers big, untracked lines for good value.
uzbekistan.beyond: Samarkand, with its turquoise domes and the Registan square, is about 2 hours from Tashkent by high-speed train. Bukhara and Khiva are further. Uzbek food is a highlight, especially *plov* (rice with meat and carrots).
uzbekistan.know:
Tashkent's airport is about 90 minutes from the resorts. Many nationalities can visit without a visa.

There's no avalanche forecast in English. Off-piste is uncontrolled.

A trip can easily combine skiing with the Silk Road cities: Tashkent, Samarkand and Bukhara. Snow is very variable, so plan the city days around it.

hunza.skiing:
Ski touring in Hunza and Naltar, in Pakistan's Karakoram, means skiing under 7,000 m giants like Rakaposhi. Naltar has a small ski area run by the Pakistan Air Force, and the valleys around offer touring from villages.

The terrain is big and largely unexplored, and the scenery is spectacular.

Naltar has a single chairlift and a few runs, but around it, ski touring opens up big, untracked terrain with views of the Karakoram. Further up the Hunza valley, touring is possible from villages under huge peaks.
hunza.beyond: Hunza's villages are famous for their apricot orchards, hospitality and the forts of Baltit and Altit, restored by the Aga Khan Trust. Attabad Lake, formed by a landslide in 2010, is a striking turquoise.
hunza.know:
Flights from Islamabad to Gilgit are often cancelled by weather; the drive along the Karakoram Highway takes about two days. Check your government's travel advice before booking.

There's no avalanche forecast, and rescue is limited. Go with a local guide.

Local guides and operators arrange everything. Lodging is simple, with guesthouses in Karimabad and Naltar.

mongoliaaltai.skiing:
Ski touring in Altai Tavan Bogd National Park, in the far west of Mongolia, means camping in gers (yurts) on the Potanin glacier, the largest in Mongolia, under Khüiten Peak (4,374 m), the country's highest. The terrain is big and open, and you'll likely be the only skiers.

The snow is dry and cold.

Days involve skiing on the broad glaciers and open slopes around the base camp, with optional climbs to summits on the border with China and Russia. The scenery is vast and empty, with nothing but ice and mountains in every direction.
mongoliaaltai.beyond: The trips are often hosted by Kazakh eagle-hunting families, who still hunt with golden eagles on horseback. The Golden Eagle Festival, in autumn, celebrates the tradition.
mongoliaaltai.know:
Fly from Ulaanbaatar to Ölgii, then drive several hours. Border-zone permits are required because the park borders China and Russia.

Spring (roughly March to May) is the best season. There's no avalanche forecast, and help is far away.

Trips are run by specialist operators who arrange permits, transport and gers. Expect very simple conditions, and be ready for cold nights.

manali.skiing:
Heli-skiing from Manali, in the Indian Himalaya, offers long descents of 1,000 m or more from high ridges in the Pir Panjal and Dhauladhar ranges. The terrain is big and varied, from open bowls to steep couloirs.

A long-running operator has been flying skiers here for decades.

Runs drop through high bowls and couloirs into the valleys, from ridges around 4,000 m, and the views of Himalayan peaks are huge. The operator uses small helicopters, flying small groups with a guide.
manali.beyond: Old Manali is a relaxed village with cafés and guesthouses, and the Hadimba Temple, built in the forest, is a beautiful wooden shrine. Tibetan monasteries and the Atal Tunnel (opened in 2020) are nearby.
manali.know:
Kullu-Manali airport has limited flights, often cancelled by weather; the drive from Delhi takes about 12 hours.

Weather can ground the helicopter for days, so allow for down days.

Trips are usually sold as a week, with lodging in Manali. Altitude matters: the helicopter can take you high quickly, so acclimatise first, ideally with a few days in Manali at around 2,000 m.

riksgransen.skiing:
Riksgränsen means "the national border", and the resort sits right on it, about 200 km north of the Arctic Circle. The lift system is modest, but that isn't the point: the treeless mountains around it are a freeride playground, with short hikes from the top lifts into bowls and couloirs, and heli drops onto bigger peaks across the border. It hosts the Scandinavian Big Mountain Championships, which says something about the terrain.

The season runs upside down. Lifts don't open until late winter, once there's enough light, and they keep going until midsummer. From late May the sun doesn't set, and the lifts run into the evening so you can ski at midnight in golden light.
riksgransen.beyond: It's a one-hotel place, and that's the charm: ski, sauna, eat, repeat. Abisko and Björkliden, half an hour down the line, add northern lights earlier in the season and the Aurora Sky Station. The ore trains rumbling past from Kiruna to Narvik are part of the soundtrack.
riksgransen.know:
Come by train: the line from Kiruna to Narvik stops right at the slope, and the night train from Stockholm connects in Kiruna. Kiruna and Evenes (Narvik) airports are each about 2 hours away.

March can still be properly cold; May is the sweet spot for corn and long days. Wind is the main hazard on open terrain, and the Swedish avalanche forecast covers the area.

kebnekaise.skiing:
This is Swedish Lapland at its biggest: Kebnekaise, the country's highest mountain, and the northern end of the Kungsleden ("the King's Trail"), with a chain of staffed huts a day's ski apart. Most trips are journeys rather than descents: long, gentle valleys, frozen lakes and passes like Tjäktja, with the option of climbing bigger peaks around the Kebnekaise mountain station.

Kebnekaise itself is shrinking, in a way. Its southern summit is a glacier cap, and it has melted enough that the rocky northern summit is now the higher of the two.
kebnekaise.beyond: Abisko sits in one of the driest, clearest pockets of the north, which makes it one of the best places on earth to see the northern lights, and the Aurora Sky Station is built for exactly that. Sámi reindeer herders use these valleys, and you may cross their tracks.
kebnekaise.know:
The night train from Stockholm stops at Abisko and Kiruna, and it's the classic way in. In winter, snowmobile taxis run from Nikkaluokta to the Kebnekaise mountain station.

The Swedish Tourist Association (STF) runs the huts. Easter is peak season, so book ahead. Wind and whiteout can be severe on the open fells, and the Swedish avalanche forecast covers Kebnekaise.

are.skiing:
Åre is Scandinavia's biggest ski resort, spread along the flanks of Åreskutan, with the village and the frozen lake at its feet. It has hosted the Alpine World Ski Championships twice (2007 and 2019), and the areas of Duved, Tegefjäll and Björnen give it the variety of a much bigger mountain. The treeless top of Åreskutan has good off-piste when the wind behaves.

Timing matters more than in the Alps. Midwinter days are short and often grey; by March the light comes back, and spring is when Åre is at its best.
are.beyond: The village is the liveliest in Sweden in winter, with a real après scene. The Åre Bergbana, a funicular from 1910, still climbs from the village, and the Åre chocolate factory is a local institution. Tännforsen, one of Sweden's largest waterfalls, is nearby and freezes into ice sculptures.
are.know:
The night train from Stockholm arrives in the village, which makes Åre one of the easiest ski trips in Europe to do by rail. Åre Östersund airport is about 1.5 hours away.

The top of the mountain is exposed to wind and fog, and upper lifts close often. The Swedish avalanche forecast covers the off-piste.

hemsedal.skiing:
Hemsedal sells itself as the "Scandinavian Alps", and by Nordic standards it earns it: steep, varied terrain off Totten, with some of the best lift-served off-piste in Norway. The valley around it is ski-touring country too, with classic tours like Skogshorn rising above the road.

Spring is the season: longer days, softer snow and the famous Norwegian Easter.
hemsedal.beyond: Hemsedal is where Oslo goes skiing, so weekends have a lively, young après scene. Easter in the Norwegian mountains (*påskefjellet*) is a national tradition, with oranges, *Kvikk Lunsj* chocolate and crime novels in the cabin.
hemsedal.know:
About 3 hours by car or bus from Oslo, or by train to Gol and then bus. Most visitors rent a cabin (*hytte*) rather than stay in a hotel, which is the Norwegian way and good value for groups. Easter week is the busiest of the year; weekdays in March are quiet.

Norway is expensive, especially eating out and alcohol, so self-catering helps. Norway's avalanche forecast (Varsom) covers the region.

lofoten.skiing:
Lofoten is a wall of jagged peaks rising straight out of the Norwegian Sea, and on skis it's pure summit-to-sea: most tours start at the shore and finish there, with the descent ending among fishing boats. Peaks are not high (often under 1,000 m), but they're steep, and the views across the sea and the other islands are hard to beat.

Some trips use sailboats as a floating base, reaching peaks without roads.
lofoten.beyond: In late winter, the skrei (Arctic cod) arrive to spawn and the islands come alive: cod hangs drying on wooden racks everywhere. Stay in a *rorbu*, the red fishermen's cabins on stilts. The Lofotr Viking Museum, in a rebuilt chieftain's longhouse, and Arctic surfing at Unstad are good rest days.
lofoten.know:
Svolvær and Leknes have airports, Evenes is a few hours' drive, and ferries cross from Bodø. A car is almost essential.

The Gulf Stream keeps Lofoten mild for its latitude, which means rain to sea level is possible and conditions swing fast. Norway's avalanche forecast covers Lofoten.

senja.skiing:
Senja, Norway's second-largest island, has everything that made Lyngen famous, with fewer people: steep peaks rising from fjords and the open sea, and tours from the road that end at the water. The outer coast is the dramatic side, with spiky ridges and quiet fishing villages.

The terrain is varied, and many tours start right from the roadside, so it's easy to pick your objective by the day's weather and snow.
senja.beyond: Tiny fishing villages like Husøy (on its own island, linked by a causeway), dramatic coastal roads and northern lights in the darker months.
senja.know:
Tromsø is the nearest major airport, a few hours' drive away; Bardufoss is closer. A car is essential, and a rented cabin in one of the outer-coast villages is the usual base, which lets you choose a different fjord each day depending on wind and snow. Guided weeks from small lodges are the alternative.

Coastal weather changes fast, and down days are part of the deal. Norway's avalanche forecast covers Senja.

narvik.skiing:
Narvikfjellet is a lift-served mountain rising straight above the town, with about 1,000 m of vertical and some of the steepest lift-accessed terrain in Norway. The views are the hook: you ski with the Ofotfjord below you, and the descents seem to drop toward the water.

It pairs perfectly with Riksgränsen, across the Swedish border: one is steep and urban, the other wild and open.
narvik.beyond: Narvik's history is unusual. It exists to ship iron ore from Kiruna, and it was the scene of fierce fighting in 1940. The Narvik War Museum tells the story. The Ofoten railway to Sweden climbs from the fjord to the high fells and is one of the most scenic train rides in Scandinavia.
narvik.know:
Evenes airport is about 1 hour away, and the train links Narvik to Riksgränsen and Kiruna, so a week can easily combine both sides of the border. In the dark early season, the slopes are floodlit; from spring the light lasts long into the evening.

The steep terrain above town is serious avalanche terrain once you leave the pistes. Norway's avalanche forecast covers the area.

sunnmore.skiing:
The Sunnmøre Alps are where Norwegian ski touring got famous: sharp peaks rising almost 1,600 m straight from the Hjørundfjord, with tours from the water to the summit and back. **Slogen** is the classic, with one of the great views in Norway from the top. **Stranda** adds lift-served freeride with fjord views.

The season runs late, and April and May are the best months.
sunnmore.beyond: The Hotel Union Øye, at the head of the Hjørundfjord, is a 19th-century hotel where European royalty once stayed. Ålesund, rebuilt in Art Nouveau style after a fire in 1904, is a beautiful town. The Geirangerfjord is nearby.
sunnmore.know:
Ålesund airport is about 1 hour away. Ferries are part of the daily routine, and some tours are reached by boat. A car is essential.

There are a few ways to do it: a rented cabin and car, which is the cheapest and most flexible; a guided week from one of the fjord hotels; or a sail-and-ski boat that moves between fjords. Coastal weather changes fast. Norway's avalanche forecast covers the area.

romsdal.skiing:
Romsdal is Norway's most dramatic valley: the Troll Wall, the tallest vertical rock face in Europe, and peaks like the Romsdalshorn and Store Vengetind rise around Åndalsnes. The skiing is steep and serious, with couloirs and big faces, and some descents end near the fjord.

It's for confident skiers who don't mind exposure, though there are gentler tours in the side valleys.
romsdal.beyond: Åndalsnes calls itself the mountaineering capital of Norway, and the Norwegian Mountaineering Centre is in town. The Romsdal Gondola climbs to a viewpoint and restaurant above the fjord, and the Rauma railway is one of Norway's most beautiful.
romsdal.know:
Molde airport is about 1 hour away; the Rauma railway arrives from Dombås. The famous Trollstigen road is closed in winter. A car and a cabin in or near Åndalsnes make the most flexible base; local guides know which couloirs are in condition.

The terrain is steep, and exposure to cliffs below many lines raises the stakes of any slide or fall. Coastal weather changes fast. Norway's avalanche forecast covers Romsdal.

jotunheimen.skiing:
Jotunheimen, "Home of the Giants", has Norway's highest mountains, including Galdhøpiggen, the highest peak in Northern Europe, and Glittertind. The terrain is high and open, with glaciers and long, rolling tours between the huts of the Norwegian Trekking Association (DNT). Lodges such as Juvasshytta and Spiterstulen make good bases for glacier day tours.

The season is spring: Easter and the weeks after it bring long days and the best snow.
jotunheimen.beyond: Easter in the mountains is a national ritual in Norway, and the huts are lively then. Lom, in the valley below, has a medieval stave church and good bakeries.
jotunheimen.know:
About 5 hours by road from Oslo, or by train to Otta and then bus. DNT huts come in three kinds: staffed, with meals; self-service, stocked with food you pay for on trust; and basic no-service huts. The self-service ones open with a DNT key, which members can borrow.

Glacier skills or a guide are needed on the glaciers. Some access roads open only in late spring. Norway's avalanche forecast covers the area.

sarek.skiing:
Sarek is Sweden's last true wilderness: no huts, no roads, no marked trails, and dozens of peaks above 1,800 m, many of them glaciated. Trips last a week or more, pulling a sled (*pulk*) and camping in the snow, through deep valleys like Rapadalen and over high passes.

This is a winter expedition, not a ski holiday, and that is the appeal.
sarek.beyond: Sarek is part of the Laponia World Heritage area, recognised both for its nature and for Sámi reindeer-herding culture. The view from Skierffe over the Rapadalen delta is one of the most famous in Sweden.
sarek.know:
Most trips start from Kvikkjokk, Ritsem or the STF mountain station at Saltoluokta. Gällivare and Kiruna are the nearest airports. You need winter camping, navigation and avalanche skills, or a guide.

Weather can be extreme, with strong winds and long storms. Reindeer herding is active here; avoid disturbing herds, especially in spring. The Swedish avalanche forecast covers parts of the area.

portillo.skiing:
Portillo is South America's most storied ski resort: a yellow hotel on the shore of the frozen Laguna del Inca, high in the Andes just below the Argentine border, with Aconcagua close by. It hosted the 1966 Alpine World Ski Championships, the first held in the Southern Hemisphere, and national teams from the north still come here to train in the northern summer.

The terrain is steep and big. Classic couloirs like the Super C are reached by a hike from the top of the lifts, and some lifts are unusual slingshot-style surface lifts, built for slopes too steep and avalanche-prone for chairs.
portillo.beyond: Life revolves around the Hotel Portillo, with a small, sociable crowd that often returns year after year, the same waiters greeting them by name. There's no town: it's the hotel, the lake and the mountains.
portillo.know:
About 2.5 hours from Santiago, on the main road to Mendoza. Stays are usually sold as Saturday-to-Saturday weekly packages, with cheaper lodge and hostel-style rooms alongside the hotel.

Big Andean storms can close the pass road for days, so leave slack at both ends. Wind slabs are common; the steep terrain outside the resort needs a guide.

tresvalles.skiing:
Three neighbouring resorts sit above Santiago: **Valle Nevado**, **La Parva** and **El Colorado**. Together they form one of the largest ski areas in the Southern Hemisphere, with wide, high, treeless terrain and big views of the Andes. The snow is often dry and the sun strong; off-piste is everywhere, and heli-skiing runs from Valle Nevado.

La Parva has a local, family feel; Valle Nevado is the most modern; El Colorado sits at the heart of the linked terrain.
tresvalles.beyond: Santiago, with its restaurants, markets and nearby wine valleys (Maipo and Casablanca), is close enough for city days between ski days. Valparaíso, with its colourful hillside streets, is about 1.5 hours to the coast.
tresvalles.know:
About 1 to 1.5 hours from Santiago, up a road with dozens of numbered hairpin bends. Weekends and Chilean school holidays (July) are very busy, and traffic up the road can crawl; some days it's restricted to one direction at certain hours.

The tops are around 3,000 m or more, so the sun and altitude hit hard. Wind slabs are the main hazard, and there's limited public avalanche forecasting, so go with a guide off-piste.

laslenas.skiing:
Las Leñas, in Mendoza province, is famous among freeriders for the **Marte** lift, which opens huge, steep terrain: long couloirs, big open faces and serious vertical. When Marte runs, it's some of the best lift-served freeride in the world, and a whole subculture of ski bums has spent seasons here for it.

The catch is the wind: Marte often closes for wind or avalanche danger, so a trip can include days of mostly piste skiing.
laslenas.beyond: A purpose-built resort with not much else around, so evenings are about long Argentine dinners that start late and steak with Malbec. Mendoza, the heart of Argentine wine country, is worth a few days before or after.
laslenas.know:
Remote: a long drive from Mendoza, with Malargüe and San Rafael as closer airports when flights run. Plan for flexibility, and consider a week rather than a few days, so you're there when Marte opens.

The snowpack is dry and wind-affected, with wind slabs and some persistent layers. The Marte terrain is big avalanche terrain: go with a local guide.

chillan.skiing:
Nevados de Chillán sits on the flanks of a volcanic complex in southern-central Chile, and catches far more snow than the resorts near Santiago. The terrain is big and open above the trees, with excellent tree skiing lower down and lots of sidecountry on the volcano's slopes.

Storms are wet and heavy, but the powder days can be excellent, and the forest gives shelter when the wind blows.
chillan.beyond: Natural hot springs are a big part of the experience, with thermal pools near the slopes. The village of Las Trancas, down the road, has cabins, restaurants and a relaxed, local feel, and is the cheaper base.
chillan.know:
About 1.5 hours from the city of Chillán, and around 5 to 6 hours from Santiago by road or train. Concepción has the nearest larger airport.

The volcanic complex has been active in recent years, so check for restrictions. Storm slabs and rain-on-snow are common hazards.

bariloche.skiing:
Cerro Catedral, near Bariloche, is one of the largest ski areas in South America, with lots of varied terrain from easy runs to steep bowls and rocky spires, and huge views down to the Nahuel Huapi lake and the Andes beyond.

The snow is maritime, and conditions vary with altitude: the top is often great while the base can be wet. The off-piste around the rock towers is excellent with a guide.
bariloche.beyond: Bariloche is a lakeside town in the Patagonian Lake District, with Swiss-style stone and timber architecture, chocolate shops on every corner, and Argentine steak and Patagonian lamb. Lakes, forests and short hikes surround it, and Cerro Otto and Campanario have famous viewpoints.
bariloche.know:
Bariloche has direct flights from Buenos Aires. July, during the Argentine winter holidays, is very busy, with Brazilian and Argentine school groups; late August and September are quieter.

Wind and storm slabs are common after storms, but the snowpack usually settles quickly.

patagoniabc.skiing:
Refugio Frey, run by Club Andino Bariloche, sits beside a small lake beneath a cluster of granite spires above Cerro Catedral. In winter it becomes a base for ski touring: couloirs between the towers, open bowls and tree runs, with dramatic rock all around.

It's a rugged, adventurous setting, and the season can run well into spring. Club Andino also runs other huts in the area, making multi-day trips possible.
patagoniabc.beyond: The granite around Frey is one of Argentina's most famous rock-climbing areas in summer. Bariloche is close for food, gear and rest days.
patagoniabc.know:
Access is on foot or ski, either from the top of Catedral's lifts or up the valley from the base. The hut is basic, with a hut keeper and simple meals; check with Club Andino Bariloche about services and booking.

There's no regular public avalanche forecast, so go with a local guide. Wind and storm slabs are the main hazards.

chilevolcanoes.skiing:
A spring trip to ski the volcanoes of Chile's Araucanía, with Pucón as the base. **Villarrica** is the classic, an active volcano with a smoking crater. **Lanín**, across the border in Argentina, is a striking, isolated cone. **Llaima** and **Lonquimay** add more choices. Each offers a climb on skins and crampons and a long descent on corn snow, with views of lakes and other volcanoes.

The cones are open and fairly uniform, but the summits can be icy, and some have crevasses.
chilevolcanoes.beyond: Pucón is an outdoor town with hot springs, lakes and forests of monkey-puzzle trees (araucarias), which give the region its name. The Mapuche people have lived here for centuries.
chilevolcanoes.know:
Villarrica's access rules change with its volcanic activity and may require a guide, so check before you go. Temuco is the nearest major airport.

Spring (roughly September to November) is the main season. Start early to catch the corn before afternoon wet slides.

ushuaia.skiing:
Cerro Castor, near Ushuaia, is one of the southernmost ski areas in the world, at the tip of South America. The resort is fairly low, but the cold, southern climate keeps the snow dry and good, and the season often runs longer than in the rest of Argentina, into October.

The terrain is varied, with views over the mountains of Tierra del Fuego. National teams from the north train here in their off-season.
ushuaia.beyond: Ushuaia is the main port for Antarctic cruises, on the Beagle Channel. Tierra del Fuego National Park, dog-sledding, cross-country skiing and king crab dinners fill rest days. The old prison, now a museum, tells the town's convict history.
ushuaia.know:
Ushuaia has direct flights from Buenos Aires. The resort is about 30 minutes from town.

The weather is windy and changeable, with temperatures near freezing. Wind slabs are the main hazard. Touring is possible in the valleys around Ushuaia with local guides.

ecuador.skiing:
Ski mountaineering on Ecuador's big volcanoes: **Cayambe**, which sits almost on the equator; **Cotopaxi**, one of the highest active volcanoes in the world; and **Chimborazo**, whose summit is the farthest point from the centre of the Earth, thanks to the bulge at the equator.

This is high-altitude climbing with skis, at well over 5,000 m. Conditions are variable, and good ski descents aren't guaranteed: you go as much for the climb and the experience as for the turns.
ecuador.beyond: Quito, at about 2,850 m, has a beautiful colonial old town and helps with acclimatisation. Haciendas, markets like Otavalo's, and the Andean highlands make good rest days.
ecuador.know:
Certified guides are required for the main volcanoes in national parks. Acclimatise slowly; altitude sickness is the main risk.

There's no avalanche forecast. Crevasses, rime ice and fast changes in snow conditions are the main hazards. The season runs all year, with some months better than others.

patagoniaicefield.skiing:
The Southern Patagonian Ice Field is one of the largest ice masses outside the polar regions, stretching about 350 km along the Andes between Argentina and Chile. Crossing it is a multi-week expedition with sleds, skis and tents, past peaks such as Fitz Roy and Cerro Torre.

It's not about the descents: it's about the journey, the wind and the wild scenery.
patagoniaicefield.beyond: El Chaltén is a small town and the trekking capital of Argentina, at the foot of Fitz Roy. The Perito Moreno glacier, in Los Glaciares National Park, is one of the most famous glaciers in the world, calving icebergs into Lago Argentino.
patagoniaicefield.know:
Expeditions need permits and registration with the national parks. Weather is extreme, with strong winds and long storms, so you need storm-proof camping and glacier skills, or a guide.

There's no avalanche forecast. El Calafate has the nearest airport.

niseko.skiing:
Niseko is where Japan's powder reputation began. Cold air off the Sea of Japan brings light snow almost every day in midwinter. Four linked resorts on Mount Niseko Annupuri (**Grand Hirafu**, **Hanazono**, **Niseko Village** and **Annupuri**) share one pass, with tree runs, bowls and night skiing, and the perfect cone of Mount Yōtei across the valley.

Off-piste is reached through **gates**: under the local Niseko Rules, you may leave the resort only through these gates, which close when the danger is high. **Rusutsu**, nearby, has excellent tree skiing and is usually quieter.
niseko.beyond: Onsen (hot spring baths) after skiing are part of the routine. Hirafu has lots of restaurants and bars, but it's very international and prices are high. For a more Japanese side, eat at a local izakaya or visit the towns of Kutchan and Otaru.
niseko.know:
New Chitose Airport, near Sapporo, is about 2 to 2.5 hours away by bus or car. Book restaurants ahead in peak season.

It's often grey and snowing, so visibility can be poor. Respect the gates and closures. Tree wells and deep-snow immersion are real risks.

sapporo.skiing:
**Kiroro** gets some of the deepest snow in Hokkaido and is much quieter than Niseko, with good tree skiing and sidecountry. Closer to the city, **Teine** (an Olympic venue in 1972) and **Sapporo Kokusai** are easy day trips, with views over the city and the sea.

Together they make a good mix of city life and powder, and you can ski a different mountain each day.
sapporo.beyond: Sapporo is a big, fun city with excellent miso ramen, crab, seafood and beer, and the Snow Festival in February, with giant ice and snow sculptures. Otaru, on the way to Kiroro, has a canal, glassworks and great sushi.
sapporo.know:
New Chitose Airport is about 1.5 hours from Kiroro. Public buses and trains link the city and resorts, so you don't need a car if you stay in Sapporo.

Daily snowfall builds storm slabs off-piste. Watch for tree wells and sluffs.

furano.skiing:
Inland Hokkaido is colder and drier than the coast, so the powder is especially light. **Furano** has long groomed runs and good tree skiing, and has hosted World Cup races. **Tomamu** and **Kamui** are quieter, and Kamui, near Asahikawa, has a cult following for its powder.

It's a good area for a road trip, with Asahidake and the Tokachi backcountry close by.

Furano also has night skiing, and the resort's long runs are a good contrast to the deep powder of the backcountry nearby.
furano.beyond: Much more Japanese than Niseko, with local izakaya and onsen. Asahikawa is known for its soy-based ramen and its zoo, and the rolling hills of Biei are beautiful under snow. Tomamu has an Ice Village of igloo bars and shops in winter.
furano.know:
Asahikawa airport is about 1 hour away; Sapporo is about 2.5 hours. A car makes it easier to move between resorts.

The colder snowpack can develop buried weak layers. Midwinter temperatures can drop very low.

asahidake.skiing:
A single ropeway climbs Asahidake, Hokkaido's highest peak, an active volcano with steaming vents. There's almost no grooming: just cold, dry powder in open terrain and birch forest, with the volcano's fumaroles hissing nearby.

The terrain is big for one lift, and it's best enjoyed with a guide who knows the routes back to the base.

The ropeway is old and small, with a single car every 15 or 20 minutes, which keeps the crowds low.
asahidake.beyond: Asahidake Onsen, at the base, has hot spring baths and a few inns. It sits in Daisetsuzan National Park, Japan's largest national park, known as "the playground of the gods" in the Ainu language.
asahidake.know:
Asahikawa airport is about 1 hour away. The ropeway can close in strong winds, and powder mornings bring queues.

Whiteouts are frequent and navigation is hard in the open terrain: it's easy to drift into the wrong valley. The cold snowpack can have weak layers; check the Japan Avalanche Network.

tokachi.skiing:
Backcountry touring in the Tokachi range and Daisetsuzan, in central Hokkaido, in famously dry snow. Popular areas such as Fukiage and Sandan-yama are reached by road, with open slopes, birch forests and bigger alpine terrain above.

The terrain suits tourers who want quiet days in cold, deep powder, with fewer people than the coast.

The Tokachi range is a chain of volcanoes, and the skiing includes open, alpine slopes above the birch forests and long tree runs lower down.
tokachi.beyond: Fukiage has a free outdoor hot spring by the trailhead, and a dip after a tour is a local ritual. Furano and Biei are nearby for rest days.
tokachi.know:
Asahikawa is the nearest airport. A car is needed. Tokachidake is an active volcano; check for restrictions. File a climbing plan before you go, as is customary in Japan.

The cold inland snowpack develops persistent weak layers more often than the coast. Go with a local guide, and check the Japan Avalanche Network.

hakuba.skiing:
Hakuba Valley has around ten resorts under the Northern Alps, including **Happo-One**, which hosted downhill races at the 1998 Nagano Olympics, as well as **Cortina**, **Tsugaike** and **Goryu**. The snow is heavy in volume, and the terrain ranges from family slopes to steep alpine bowls.

Above the resorts, the Hakuba mountains offer serious backcountry with big lines. Cortina has some of the best tree skiing in Japan.
hakuba.beyond: The town has lots of restaurants, bars and onsen. The snow monkeys of Jigokudani, which bathe in hot springs, and Nagano city with the Zenko-ji temple are within day-trip distance.
hakuba.know:
From Tokyo, take the Hokuriku Shinkansen to Nagano, then a bus to Hakuba: about 3 to 4 hours in total. Shuttles link the resorts.

Very heavy snowfall loads slopes quickly, causing storm slabs and glide cracks. The big alpine terrain needs a guide. Check the Japan Avalanche Network.

hakkoda.skiing:
A ropeway climbs into the Hakkoda mountains, giving access to backcountry among the famous "snow monsters": trees coated in thick rime ice. The snow is deep and cold, and there are few foreign skiers.

The terrain is mostly moderate, but navigation is the main challenge in frequent whiteouts. It pairs well with Zao, further south, which is also known for snow monsters.
hakkoda.beyond: Sukayu Onsen, at the foot of the mountains, is a famous old hot spring with a huge wooden mixed bath. Aomori city has excellent seafood and the Nebuta Museum, with giant paper lanterns from the summer festival.
hakkoda.know:
Aomori airport is about 1 hour away. Guides are strongly recommended because the terrain is hard to navigate in whiteout.

In 1902, a military exercise here ended in disaster when soldiers were lost in a blizzard: a reminder of how severe the weather can be.

tateyama.skiing:
The Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route crosses the Northern Alps and opens in mid-April, giving access to huge couloirs and open slopes from mountain huts at Murodo. It's spring skiing on a deep snowpack, with big views of the Northern Alps.

The terrain ranges from moderate slopes near Murodo to steep, serious couloirs on peaks such as Tsurugi.

Huts and lodges around Murodo are bases for multi-day trips, with tours onto Oyama, the main summit of Tateyama, and the surrounding ridges.
tateyama.beyond: The snow walls along the road at Murodo can reach many metres tall, and walking between them is a famous sight. The Kurobe Dam is one of the largest in Japan.
tateyama.know:
The Alpine Route is mainly a sightseeing route, with buses and cable cars. Toyama airport is about 1.5 hours away. Book huts ahead in Golden Week (late April to early May).

Wet-snow avalanches and cornice collapses are the main spring hazards. Weather can turn fast in the high Alps.

fuji.skiing:
In late spring, you can climb Mount Fuji, Japan's highest and most sacred peak, and ski from near the crater rim: a descent of around 1,500 m with views across the country.

The snow is often hard and icy, especially early in the day, and a slip can be fatal on the long, uniform slopes. Timing the snow softening is everything.
fuji.beyond: The Fuji Five Lakes, at the foot of the mountain, have onsen, views and good food. Tokyo is close for a city day.
fuji.know:
The official climbing season is in summer, so the mountain has no services in spring. File a climbing plan before you go.

Crampons and an ice axe are essential. Turn around if the snow is too hard or the weather turns. Winds near the summit can be extreme.

Most skiers climb from the Fujinomiya or Subashiri side; check road access, as some roads open only in spring. Go with a guide if you're new to steep, icy snow.

svalbard.skiing:
Svalbard is a high-arctic archipelago, about halfway between mainland Norway and the North Pole, where glaciers cover more than half the land. Ski touring here means glaciers, wide valleys and peaks rising from frozen fjords, reached on foot from Longyearbyen, by snowmobile, or from expedition boats later in spring as the sea ice breaks up.

The terrain is mostly moderate. The adventure is the remoteness, the light and the arctic setting rather than steep skiing.
svalbard.beyond: Longyearbyen is one of the northernmost towns in the world, a former coal-mining settlement with a few good restaurants, the Svalbard Museum and the Global Seed Vault nearby. From late April the sun never sets. There are more polar bears in the archipelago than people.
svalbard.know:
Flights come from Oslo and Tromsø. Polar bears are a real danger: outside the settlements you must carry protection against them, which is why most trips are guided. Some travel must be reported to the Governor of Svalbard, and there are strict rules about disturbing wildlife.

The snowpack is thin and wind-affected, with weak layers. Glaciers have crevasses. Norway's Varsom forecasts the Longyearbyen area.

sources.label: Travel rules and notification (Governor of Svalbard)

trollpeninsula.skiing:
The Troll Peninsula (Tröllaskagi), in north Iceland, is a mass of steep mountains between fjords, with descents that run from summits of around 1,000 to 1,500 m almost down to the sea. It was one of the first places in Europe to offer heli-skiing on sea-level-to-summit terrain, and it's also excellent for touring, sometimes from boats.

Spring brings very long days, so you can ski late into the evening, and by May the light barely fades.
trollpeninsula.beyond: Geothermal pools are everywhere, from town swimming pools to hot springs with fjord views; soaking in one after skiing is the local après. Akureyri is a small, lively town with good restaurants. Whale watching runs from fishing villages like Dalvík and Hauganes, and Siglufjörður has a museum about the herring boom.
trollpeninsula.know:
Akureyri airport is about 1 hour away, with flights from Reykjavík; driving from Reykjavík takes about 5 hours. A car helps.

The weather is very changeable, so expect some down days. The Icelandic Met Office forecasts avalanche danger for north Iceland.

westfjords.skiing:
The Westfjords are a remote corner of Iceland, cut by deep fjords and steep, flat-topped mountains. The classic trip is a week of ski touring from a sailboat: skiing from summits down to the shore, then sailing to the next fjord, often with no road or house in sight.

The terrain is varied, from open slopes to steep couloirs, and the views of the fjords and the Greenland Sea are spectacular.
westfjords.beyond: Ísafjörður is the main town, with a lively Easter ski week and a free music festival. The Hornstrandir nature reserve, to the north, is uninhabited and home to arctic foxes.
westfjords.know:
Ísafjörður has flights from Reykjavík, though they're often cancelled by weather; the drive is long and winding. Most visitors join a sail-and-ski trip or stay in Ísafjörður with a guide.

The weather is wild and windy. The Westfjords have a long history of avalanches: in 1995, avalanches hit the villages of Súðavík and Flateyri, killing more than 30 people. The Icelandic Met Office forecasts the region.

westgreenland.skiing:
Ski touring in the empty fjords of West Greenland, around Maniitsoq and Sisimiut, usually from an expedition yacht or by helicopter. Peaks rise straight from the sea to 1,000 to 2,000 m, and many slopes have rarely or never been skied.

Spring weather is often cold and stable, with long days, and the skiing ends at the shoreline among icebergs.
westgreenland.beyond: Maniitsoq is called the "Venice of the Arctic" for its channels. Sisimiut has a strong Inuit culture and dog-sledding, and hosts the Arctic Circle Race, one of the toughest cross-country ski races in the world. Near Kangerlussuaq, musk oxen roam the tundra.
westgreenland.know:
International flights reach Nuuk and Kangerlussuaq, then boats or helicopters continue. Trips are expensive and need booking well ahead, usually with a specialist operator.

There's no public avalanche forecast, so go guided. Wind slabs are the main hazard, and rescue can be very far away.

eastgreenland.skiing:
The Ammassalik Alps, around Tasiilaq, are a range of jagged peaks above sea ice and icebergs on Greenland's remote east coast. Touring and heli-skiing here mean steep coastal peaks, glaciers and couloirs, with the frozen sea below.

It's very remote and wild, with few people and no infrastructure beyond the town.
eastgreenland.beyond: Tasiilaq is a small Inuit town of brightly painted houses, where hunting, fishing and dog-sledding are still part of daily life. The icebergs and sea ice are spectacular, and in spring, dog-sled trips across the sea ice are possible.
eastgreenland.know:
Flights go to Kulusuk from Reykjavík, then by helicopter or boat to Tasiilaq. Most trips are run by specialist operators, with local hunters often providing transport.

The piteraq, a powerful wind that falls from the ice cap, can be extremely strong. There's no public avalanche forecast; go guided.

Trips usually run in spring (March to May), when the days are long and the sea ice is still there. Book well ahead, as group sizes are small.

baffin.skiing:
Around Clyde River and Sam Ford Fjord, on Baffin Island, huge granite walls rise from the sea ice, with couloirs of around 1,000 m running between them. Teams camp on the sea ice and travel by snowmobile with Inuit outfitters.

It's one of the most remote and dramatic ski destinations in the world, visited by only a handful of teams each spring, and it featured in some famous ski films.
baffin.beyond: Clyde River is a small Inuit community. The trip is a chance to learn about life in the Arctic from the people who live there, and the outfitters' knowledge of ice and weather is essential.
baffin.know:
Flights go to Iqaluit, then to Clyde River. Arrange local outfitters well ahead. Polar bear protection is essential.

April is very cold; by mid-May there's 24-hour daylight. There's no avalanche forecast, so you need full self-reliance.

greenlandcrossing.skiing:
Crossing the Greenland ice cap is the classic polar ski journey: about 550 km from coast to coast, usually around four weeks, pulling a heavy sled across the vast, flat ice to a high point of about 2,500 m. Fridtjof Nansen made the first crossing in 1888, and modern teams follow much the same line.

It's not about descents. It's about endurance, cold and the emptiness of the ice.
greenlandcrossing.beyond: The endless white of the ice cap, the silence, the long light and the moment you reach the far coast and see rock again.
greenlandcrossing.know:
Expeditions need permission from the Greenland authorities, including proof of rescue insurance. Most teams start from the east coast (via Kulusuk) and finish near Kangerlussuaq. Guided crossings are available from specialist operators.

Crevasses near the coasts, piteraq storms and cold injuries are the main risks. Nights can reach −30 °C in spring.

vatnajokull.skiing:
Vatnajökull is the largest ice cap in Iceland and one of the largest in Europe. Crossing it takes a week or more, pulling sleds over the ice, past active volcanoes buried under the glacier, such as Grímsvötn, which erupts every few years. A hut run by the Iceland Glaciological Society on the rim of Grímsvötn is a famous stop.

The terrain is mostly flat to rolling, and the challenge is the weather and the distance.
vatnajokull.beyond: Vatnajökull National Park includes the Jökulsárlón glacier lagoon, where icebergs drift to the sea, and Hvannadalshnúkur, Iceland's highest peak. Hot springs are a good reward at the end.
vatnajokull.know:
Keflavík airport is the starting point. A few guided groups go each spring. Fast-moving Atlantic storms can pin you down for days.

Avalanche exposure is low, but crevasses, whiteouts and storms are the main risks. Good navigation and storm-proof camping are essential.

snowymtns.skiing:
The Snowy Mountains of New South Wales hold Australia's biggest resorts. **Perisher** is the largest, spread over several linked areas, with wide, rolling terrain among snow gums. **Thredbo** has the most vertical in Australia and the highest lift-served point, with long runs from the top of the Kosciuszko Express. **Charlotte Pass**, the highest resort village, is reached only by snowcat in winter.

The natural snow is variable, and rain is possible even in midwinter, so snowmaking matters. On a good day after a storm, the snow gum glades are a uniquely Australian experience.
snowymtns.beyond: Jindabyne, on its lake, is the main town, with restaurants and a relaxed feel. Wombats and kangaroos are common, and the snow gums, twisted and multicoloured, are beautiful in themselves.
snowymtns.know:
Canberra is about 2.5 hours away; Sydney is about 6 hours. The Skitube, a rack railway, runs from Bullocks Flat to Perisher and Blue Cow, avoiding the road. A national park entry fee applies, and chains are required in season.

School holidays and weekends are very busy. Perisher is on the Epic Pass and Thredbo on the Ikon Pass.

mainrange.skiing:
The Main Range is the roof of Australia, a high, treeless ridge that includes Mount Kosciuszko (2,228 m), the country's highest peak. Day tours and overnight trips start from Thredbo or Charlotte Pass, onto rolling plateaus, glacial lakes like Blue Lake, and peaks like Mount Townsend.

The **Western Faces** are the highlight: long, steep slopes dropping more than 1,000 m toward the Geehi valley, which feel more like New Zealand than Australia.
mainrange.beyond: Seaman's Hut, a small stone shelter on the range, was built in memory of two skiers who died in a blizzard in 1928. Snow camping under the stars on the Main Range is an unforgettable experience.
mainrange.know:
Canberra is the nearest airport. Fill in a trip-intentions form with the national park, and carry a personal locator beacon.

The weather on the Main Range can be extreme, with blizzards and whiteouts arriving fast. Australia has no government avalanche service, but the Mountain Safety Collective, a non-profit, publishes backcountry forecasts for the main alpine areas. Avalanches do happen, especially on the Western Faces and under cornices.

victoria.skiing:
Three resorts in the Victorian Alps serve Melbourne. **Mt Buller**, the closest, has a big village and a good variety of terrain. **Mt Hotham** is an "upside-down" resort, with the village on the ridge and runs dropping below it, and has the most expert terrain in Australia. **Falls Creek** is a ski-in, ski-out village with wide, rolling runs and access to the Bogong High Plains.

The snow is variable, and snowmaking keeps the season going.
victoria.beyond: Falls Creek hosts the Kangaroo Hoppet, a cross-country race on the Bogong High Plains that's part of the international Worldloppet series. Mansfield and Bright are pleasant country towns, with good food and wine in the valleys.
victoria.know:
Melbourne is about 3 to 4.5 hours away. Carrying chains is mandatory in the alpine areas during the season. A resort entry fee applies.

School holidays and weekends are very busy. Falls Creek and Mt Hotham are on the Epic Pass.

queenstown.skiing:
Four resorts surround Queenstown and Wanaka. **The Remarkables** has dramatic views and good freeride chutes. **Coronet Peak**, New Zealand's first commercial ski field, has night skiing and is closest to town. **Cardrona** is big, family-friendly and known for its parks. **Treble Cone** has the biggest vertical in the area and steep, natural terrain with views over Lake Wanaka.

Heli-skiing is available from both towns.
queenstown.beyond: Queenstown is New Zealand's adventure capital, where commercial bungy jumping began on the Kawarau Bridge. Central Otago is famous for its pinot noir, and Arrowtown, a historic gold-rush town, is a short drive away. Wanaka is calmer.
queenstown.know:
Queenstown has an international airport with flights from Australia. The ski fields have no lodging on the mountain; you drive up each day, often on gravel roads where chains may be needed.

The NZ Avalanche Advisory forecasts the backcountry.

Many skiers combine Queenstown and Wanaka in one trip, staying in each for a few days. Rental cars are the best way to get around.

mthutt.skiing:
Mt Hutt is a big, open bowl high above the Canterbury Plains, with views across to the Pacific Ocean. It's often the first ski field in New Zealand to open, thanks to its altitude and snowmaking, and the terrain is wide and varied, from cruising runs to steep chutes on the edges.

Wind is the main challenge: Mt Hutt closes more often than most for wind.

The terrain includes the South Face, with steep chutes, and wide, groomed runs in the main bowl. On clear days, you can see the Pacific and the Canterbury Plains below.
mthutt.beyond: Methven, at the bottom of the mountain, is a small farming town with a friendly, laid-back feel and new hot pools. Jet-boating in the Rakaia Gorge is a classic outing.
mthutt.know:
Christchurch is about 1.5 hours away. The access road is steep and gravel; chains may be needed. There's no lodging on the mountain, so most people stay in Methven.

Heli-skiing runs from Methven. The NZ Avalanche Advisory covers the area.

clubfields.skiing:
New Zealand's club fields are a unique skiing experience: small, non-profit ski areas run by clubs, with **rope tows** that you grip with a "nutcracker" clamp on a harness belt. **Craigieburn** has steep, ungroomed terrain and famous chutes; **Broken River** is linked to it by a traverse; **Temple Basin**, at Arthur's Pass, is reached by a hike up from the road.

The terrain is steep and natural, and the crowds are small.
clubfields.beyond: Club lodges offer cheap, simple accommodation, with communal meals and shared chores. The kea, an inquisitive mountain parrot, is a regular visitor (and likes to steal things). The limestone boulders of Castle Hill are nearby.
clubfields.know:
Christchurch is about 2 hours away. The roads are rough and often require 4WD or chains. The rope tows take practice; most fields offer a lesson.

The NZ Avalanche Advisory covers the area. The terrain is steep and natural, so avalanche awareness is important.

nzheli.skiing:
Heli-skiing is a big part of New Zealand skiing, with operators in Wanaka, Queenstown and Methven flying skiers into the Southern Alps for big days of powder or corn.

The other classic is the **Tasman Glacier**, New Zealand's longest, under Aoraki/Mount Cook. Ski planes land on the glacier for long runs among the icefalls and seracs of the highest mountains in the country.
nzheli.beyond: Aoraki/Mount Cook (3,724 m) is New Zealand's highest peak, and the village has the Sir Edmund Hillary Alpine Centre. The Aoraki Mackenzie International Dark Sky Reserve has some of the clearest night skies in the world, and Lake Tekapo's tiny stone church is a famous sight.
nzheli.know:
Operators are based in Wanaka, Queenstown, Methven and Mount Cook. Book ahead, but expect weather days.

The NZ Avalanche Advisory covers the area. Glacier travel has crevasse risks, so go with a guide.

ruapehu.skiing:
Mount Ruapehu, an active volcano in the centre of the North Island, has two ski fields: **Whakapapa**, on the north side, and **Tūroa**, on the south side, with one of the biggest verticals in Australasia. The terrain is volcanic, with ridges, gullies and lava formations. Touring to the summit plateau and the steaming Crater Lake is a classic.

The lift company collapsed in 2022, and both fields now have new owners, so check what's operating before you go.
ruapehu.beyond: Tongariro National Park, New Zealand's first, was gifted by a Māori chief in 1887 and is a dual UNESCO World Heritage site, for its natural and cultural values. Mount Ngauruhoe, nearby, stood in for Mount Doom in *The Lord of the Rings*.
ruapehu.know:
Auckland is about 4.5 hours away; Taupō is closer. The weather is changeable, with wind, rime ice and whiteouts.

Check the volcanic alert level on GeoNet. The NZ Avalanche Advisory covers the area.

alyeska.skiing:
Alyeska, in Girdwood, has a base near sea level and steep upper bowls, so you can ski from alpine terrain down to sea views over Turnagain Arm. A tram climbs to the upper mountain, and the terrain is steep and varied, with long runs and deep coastal snow.

It pairs well with backcountry at Turnagain Pass, about 40 minutes south, and with heli and cat skiing in the Chugach.

The upper mountain has steep bowls and chutes, and the lower mountain has long, wooded runs. The views of Turnagain Arm and the Chugach are spectacular on clear days.
alyeska.beyond: Girdwood is a funky little town with good food and a strong local community. The Alyeska Nordic Spa is a good rest day, and the northern lights can appear on clear winter nights.
alyeska.know:
Anchorage airport is about 45 minutes away. Midwinter days are very short, around 5 to 6 hours of daylight in December; late winter and spring have much more light.

The Chugach National Forest Avalanche Information Center forecasts the backcountry.

chugach.skiing:
Valdez and the Chugach Mountains are the home of the steep spines you see in ski films: coastal Alaska snow sticks to 50° faces in a way it rarely does elsewhere. Thompson Pass, above Valdez, is one of the snowiest places in Alaska, and heli operators fly skiers onto huge, steep lines.

The World Extreme Skiing Championships were held here in the 1990s, and the area still has a wild, pioneering feel.
chugach.beyond: Valdez is a small port town, rebuilt after the original was destroyed in the 1964 earthquake. Each spring, Tailgate Alaska brings a festival of skiers and snowboarders in RVs to Thompson Pass.
chugach.know:
Valdez has a small airport with flights from Anchorage; the drive takes about 5 hours. Heli-skiing is very weather-dependent, so plan for at least a week and expect down days.

Avalanche hazards are serious on steep terrain. Operators run professional avalanche programs.

haines.skiing:
Haines is Alaska's other heli mecca: big glaciated lines in the Chilkat Range, quieter and smaller than Valdez. The terrain includes steep spines, big faces and long glacier runs, and it has featured in many ski films.

It's a smaller, more intimate operation than Valdez, with fewer people and plenty of terrain.
haines.beyond: Haines is a small town known for its arts community and quirky Hammer Museum. Each autumn, the Chilkat Bald Eagle Preserve hosts one of the largest gatherings of bald eagles in the world. Tlingit culture is strong in the area.
haines.know:
Fly to Juneau, then take a ferry or small plane to Haines. The Haines Highway connects to Canada's Yukon.

Heli-skiing is very weather-dependent, so allow for down days. Operators run professional avalanche programs.

Haines is small, with simple lodges and a few restaurants. A week is the usual minimum to have a chance at good flying weather.

denali.skiing:
Denali (6,190 m) is North America's highest peak, and skiing it is a serious expedition of about three weeks, usually via the West Buttress. Some teams ski from high on the mountain, but it's as much a mountaineering trip as a ski trip.

For most skiers, the **Ruth Gorge** is the more accessible option: ski touring on a glacier under granite walls over 1,500 m high, with a mountain hut on a nunatak in the middle of the glacier.
denali.beyond: Talkeetna, the gateway town, is a quirky place famous for its bush pilots, and once had a cat as its honorary mayor. Flightseeing over the Alaska Range is spectacular.
denali.know:
Fly from Talkeetna by ski plane to the glaciers. Climbers on Denali must register with the National Park Service at least 60 days ahead and pay a mountaineering fee.

The weather can be extreme, with storms that last days. You need glacier skills and high-altitude experience, or a guide.

tremblant.skiing:
Mont-Tremblant, in the Laurentians, is the flagship resort of eastern North America, with runs on several sides of the mountain and a colourful pedestrian village at the base. The terrain is mostly intermediate, with glades on the Edge side and a few steep runs.

It's cold, often very cold, and the snow can be firm, but the village and atmosphere make it special.

The south side gets the sun and the views over the lake; the north side is colder but often has better snow. The Edge side has some of the best glades in eastern Canada.
tremblant.beyond: The village has a French-Canadian feel, with Québécois food like poutine and tourtière. The Scandinave Spa, nearby, offers outdoor Nordic baths in the forest. In March, sugar shacks (*cabanes à sucre*) serve maple-syrup feasts.
tremblant.know:
Montréal is about 1.5 hours away. Pack for real cold: windchill below −30 °C is common in January.

The resort is on the Ikon Pass.

vermont.skiing:
Northern Vermont has the best snow in the US Northeast, with classic New England tree skiing. **Stowe**, on Mount Mansfield, has the famous "Front Four", steep, narrow trails. **Jay Peak**, near the Canadian border, gets the most snow in the East, thanks to the "Jay Cloud". **Sugarbush** has varied terrain and a laid-back vibe, and **Mad River Glen** next door is a skiers-only cooperative with a single chair: "Ski it if you can".

The snow can be icy, but powder days in the trees are excellent.
vermont.beyond: The Trapp Family Lodge, near Stowe, was founded by the family from *The Sound of Music*. Ben & Jerry's factory, maple syrup, Vermont cheddar and craft beer are local highlights.
vermont.know:
Burlington airport is about 1 hour away; Montréal is about 2 hours. Freeze-thaw cycles make conditions variable.

The backcountry is mostly in the trees; the Vermont Backcountry Alliance maintains glades.

tuckerman.skiing:
Tuckerman Ravine, on Mount Washington, is the classic Eastern spring pilgrimage. Each spring, skiers hike up to the ravine to ski its steep headwall, with slopes of around 50°, while crowds watch from a pile of boulders called Lunch Rocks.

In 1939, Toni Matt famously schussed the headwall in a race, and the ravine has drawn skiers since the 1930s.

Beyond the headwall, the ravine has gullies like Left Gully and Hillman's Highway, which offer slightly gentler options. The atmosphere on a sunny spring weekend is part party, part pilgrimage.
tuckerman.beyond: Mount Washington held the world record for the highest wind speed measured at the surface for decades, about 372 km/h in 1934. The Appalachian Mountain Club's Joe Dodge Lodge, at Pinkham Notch, is the base.
tuckerman.know:
Portland and Boston are the nearest major airports. The hike up from Pinkham Notch takes about 2 to 3 hours.

The ravine has serious hazards: falling ice, crevasses, undermined snow and avalanches. The Mount Washington Avalanche Center forecasts the ravine.

chicchocs.skiing:
The Chic-Chocs, in Gaspésie National Park, get eastern Canada's best snow, with open alpine bowls and glades above the St. Lawrence River. Peaks like Mont Albert and Mont Jacques-Cartier offer big terrain by eastern standards, and huts and lodges make multi-day trips possible.

The terrain is surprisingly alpine, with treeless summits and long descents.

The Chic-Chocs Mountain Lodge offers guided touring and cat-skiing from a lodge in the park, while the park's huts allow independent trips. The snow is often deep, thanks to storms from the St. Lawrence.
chicchocs.beyond: The Gaspésie is a beautiful, remote corner of Québec, with fishing villages, seafood and the famous Percé Rock. The park is home to the last herd of woodland caribou south of the St. Lawrence, and some areas are closed to protect them.
chicchocs.know:
The drive from Montréal is long, around 8 hours; Mont-Joli has the nearest airport. The Chic-Chocs Mountain Lodge and the park's huts need booking.
