Avalanche Québec forecasts the Chic-Chocs. Weather can be severe, with strong winds and whiteouts.

grosmorne.skiing:
Gros Morne National Park, on Newfoundland's west coast, has fjords, tablelands and treeless bowls with big, open terrain. The snow can be deep, and the setting is wild and remote, with few people.

Marble Mountain, in the Humber Valley near Corner Brook, offers lift-served skiing for stormy days.

The backcountry ranges from the barren, orange-rock Tablelands to steep gullies above the fjords of Bonne Bay. Marble Mountain, near Corner Brook, has about 500 m of vertical and some good glades.
grosmorne.beyond: Gros Morne is a UNESCO World Heritage site, partly because the Tablelands expose rock from the Earth's mantle. Newfoundland is famous for its hospitality, kitchen parties and "screech-in" ceremonies for visitors.
grosmorne.know:
Deer Lake airport is about 1 hour from the park. A car is essential.

There's no regular avalanche forecast for the area. The weather is maritime and can change quickly. Go with a local guide.

Rocky Harbour and Woody Point are small villages in the park; lodging is limited in winter, so book ahead. Local guides run backcountry trips and know where the snow is best.

maunakea.skiing:
Mauna Kea, on Hawaii's Big Island, rises to about 4,200 m and gets snow after rare winter storms. Skiing here means driving up in a 4x4 and skiing short runs on thin snow over volcanic rock, then surfing the same day.

It's an opportunistic trip: you go only when it snows, and conditions are often thin.

The skiing is short and opportunistic, with thin snow over lava. Most people come for the novelty and the views of the Pacific and Mauna Loa.
maunakea.beyond: Mauna Kea is sacred to Native Hawaiians, and the summit has world-class observatories. Respect the cultural significance of the mountain and stay on established routes.
maunakea.know:
Kona and Hilo are about 2 hours away. A 4x4 is needed beyond the visitor centre. The road can close in storms or ice.

The altitude is high and you drive up from sea level quickly, so altitude sickness is a real risk.

antarctica.skiing:
Ski touring on the Antarctic Peninsula, from expedition yachts or small ships, among icebergs, penguins and whales. Peaks rise straight from the sea, and descents end at the shoreline, where zodiacs wait to take you back to the boat.

It's the trip of a lifetime, and the scenery is unlike anywhere else on Earth.

Days are spent touring from anchorages, with short to medium climbs and long descents back to the sea. Small groups and expert guides keep it safe.
antarctica.beyond: Gentoo and Adélie penguins, seals and humpback whales are common. Port Lockroy, a former British base, has a museum and post office.
antarctica.know:
Most trips leave from Ushuaia and cross the Drake Passage, about two days each way, which can be rough. Some trips fly to King George Island instead.

Visitors follow strict rules set by IAATO, including biosecurity and keeping distance from wildlife. Crevasses are a real hazard, and rescue is very far away.

Trips are expensive and book up a year or more ahead. November offers the best snow; later in the season, the snow becomes wetter.

grandvalira.skiing:
Grandvalira is the biggest ski area in the Pyrenees, spread across Andorra from Pas de la Casa on the French border to Soldeu and El Tarter. The terrain is mostly wide, rolling intermediate runs above the treeline, with good tree skiing lower down and some off-piste.

Soldeu hosted the World Cup Finals in 2019, and the ski schools are known for teaching in English.

The area includes several sectors: Pas de la Casa is the party town by the French border; Soldeu and El Tarter are quieter, with good tree runs. Ordino Arcalís, also in Andorra, is the place for freeride.
grandvalira.beyond: Andorra is a small, mountainous country with duty-free shopping in Andorra la Vella. The Caldea spa is a huge thermal complex with outdoor pools. Catalan is the official language.
grandvalira.know:
Barcelona and Toulouse are about 3 hours away; there's no major airport in Andorra. Prices are reasonable compared with the Alps.

Snowmaking is extensive. Andorra's weather service publishes avalanche information.

Lift passes and lodging are good value, and the ski-school packages are popular with British families. Easter and February holidays are busy.

baqueira.skiing:
Baqueira-Beret, in the Val d'Aran, is Spain's best ski resort, on the Atlantic-facing side of the Pyrenees, so it gets more snow than most of the range. The terrain is big and varied, with wide pistes and lots of off-piste across three areas: Baqueira, Beret and Bonaigua.

It's a favourite of the Spanish royal family.

The off-piste is the highlight, with big, open terrain off the Baqueira and Beret areas and quieter slopes on the Bonaigua side. Spanish skiers come for long weekends, and the slopes are quietest midweek.
baqueira.beyond: The Val d'Aran has its own language, Aranese (a form of Occitan), and its own culture. Try the *olla aranesa*, a hearty stew. Dinners start late, Spanish style. Vielha is the main town, and the valley has beautiful Romanesque churches.
baqueira.know:
Toulouse is about 2.5 hours away; Barcelona about 4 hours. Spanish holidays and weekends are busy.

The Val d'Aran has its own avalanche service (Lauegi).

pyreneeshr.skiing:
The Pyrenees Haute Route crosses the central Pyrenees from Gavarnie to the Aneto, the highest peak in the range at 3,404 m, staying in mountain huts on both sides of the French-Spanish border. The route passes peaks like the Vignemale and Monte Perdido, and is quieter than its Alpine cousin.

The glaciers are small, but the terrain is big and wild.

The route crosses the border several times, from French valleys to Spanish ones, with big views of the range. The days are long but the glaciers are small, so it's less technical than the Alpine Haute Route.
pyreneeshr.beyond: The Cirque de Gavarnie, a huge amphitheatre of cliffs, and the Ordesa canyon are part of a UNESCO World Heritage site. Spanish huts serve late, hearty dinners.
pyreneeshr.know:
Toulouse, Zaragoza and Barcelona are about 3 hours from the start. Spring (roughly March to May) is the season. Some huts have only self-service winter rooms, so check before you go.

Météo-France and Spain's weather service publish avalanche bulletins.

tatras.skiing:
The High Tatras are a compact granite range on the border between Slovakia and Poland, with steep couloirs, sharp ridges and alpine lakes. On the Polish side, the cable car to Kasprowy Wierch gives access to classic terrain; on the Slovak side, the Lomnický štít cable car climbs to one of the highest peaks.

Touring from mountain huts (*chaty*) is a classic way to explore.

The Tatras are steep and dramatic for their size, with couloirs and big faces that feel alpine. Kasprowy Wierch, on the Polish side, is one of the most popular freeride spots in Poland, and the Slovak side has quieter touring.
tatras.beyond: Zakopane, on the Polish side, is a lively mountain town with wooden architecture and *góral* culture, including smoked sheep's cheese (*oscypek*). Kraków is about 2 hours away.
tatras.know:
Kraków and Poprad are the nearest airports. National park rules restrict ski touring to certain areas and times, so check them first.

The Slovak and Polish rescue services publish avalanche bulletins.

popova.skiing:
Popova Šapka, in the Šar Mountains above Tetovo, runs one of Europe's longest-running cat-skiing operations. The terrain is wide and wild, with open bowls and long descents across a range of peaks reaching over 2,700 m.

The resort itself is small and old-fashioned, but the cat skiing opens big, empty terrain.

The cats climb to ridges well above the resort, opening long, open descents with views across the Polog valley. The operation offers good value, and groups are small.
popova.beyond: Tetovo's Painted Mosque is one of the most beautiful in the Balkans. Skopje, the capital, has an old bazaar, and Lake Ohrid, a UNESCO site, is a few hours away. Macedonian food is hearty: try *tavče gravče* (baked beans) and *ajvar* (pepper relish).
popova.know:
Skopje airport is about 1 hour away. Prices are low.

There's no public avalanche forecast, so ski with the operators' guides.

Lodging at Popova Šapka is simple, with a few hotels. Tetovo and Skopje are close for city days.

pirin.skiing:
Bansko sits at the foot of the Pirin Mountains, a UNESCO-listed national park with alpine limestone and marble peaks up to Vihren (2,914 m). The resort has a gondola from town and good pistes, and the surrounding mountains offer touring from huts.

Bansko is cheap and lively, and the touring is quiet and wild.

For tourers, Vihren's marble faces and the cirques around the Vihren and Banderitsa huts are the highlights, with steep gullies and wide, open bowls. The resort has hosted women's World Cup races, and its long ski road down to town is a classic end to the day.
pirin.beyond: Bansko's old town has stone houses and traditional taverns (*mehanas*) serving hearty dishes like *kapama* (slow-cooked meat). The Rila Monastery, a UNESCO site, is about 1.5 hours away.
pirin.know:
Sofia is about 2.5 hours away. Prices are low compared with the Alps.

The Bulgarian mountain rescue service publishes avalanche information.

Bansko gets busy in February, and the gondola queues from town can be long in the morning; staying near the lift or starting early helps. Guides in Bansko can arrange hut-to-hut tours in the national park.

scotland.skiing:
Scotland's Highlands have wild, wind-scoured plateaus and gullies, with five ski areas (Cairngorm, Glenshee, The Lecht, Nevis Range and Glencoe) and backcountry touring when conditions allow. The Cairngorms plateau feels Arctic, and Ben Nevis has steep gullies.

The snow is unpredictable, but when it's on, Scottish skiing can be brilliant.

Ski touring on the Cairngorms plateau feels closer to the Arctic than to the Alps: vast, rounded, and often swept by wind into hard snow and cornices. On the west coast, Glencoe, Scotland's oldest commercial ski area, sits at the edge of Rannoch Moor, and the Nevis Range gondola gives access to the steep back corries of Aonach Mòr.
scotland.beyond: Whisky distilleries, bothies (simple mountain shelters) and Highland hospitality. The Cairngorms have the only free-ranging reindeer herd in the UK.
scotland.know:
Inverness and Glasgow are the nearest airports. The weather is notoriously windy; Cairngorm summit has recorded gusts of about 280 km/h.

The Scottish Avalanche Information Service forecasts six areas daily.

There are several ways to do it: chase forecasts and drive up for a weekend when snow arrives, base yourself in Aviemore or Fort William with a local guide, or combine a lift day with a touring day. Navigation skills matter: on the plateau, whiteouts and cornices catch people every winter.

oukaimeden.skiing:
Oukaïmeden, in Morocco's High Atlas, has the highest lift-served slopes in Africa, with a chairlift reaching about 3,200 m and a handful of drag lifts. The terrain is open and wide above the treeline, and after a good storm the off-piste on the surrounding slopes can be excellent.

The lifts and rental gear are basic, and the snow varies a lot from year to year. Local men offer donkey rides back up the slopes, which is part of the charm.
oukaimeden.beyond: Prehistoric rock engravings are scattered around the plateau. Marrakech, about 1.5 hours away, has the Jemaa el-Fna square, the souks, riads and some of the best food in North Africa: tagines, couscous and mint tea.
oukaimeden.know:
Marrakech has flights from all over Europe. Hire a driver or take a grand taxi up the mountain road.

Check snow conditions before going, as the season can be short. There's no avalanche forecast.

highatlas.skiing:
Ski touring in the High Atlas means climbing Toubkal (4,167 m), the highest peak in North Africa, from the Berber village of Imlil, with mules carrying the gear to the Toubkal refuge. From the huts, couloirs and open slopes lead to Toubkal and other 4,000 m peaks.

The snow is variable, but in a good year the touring is big, wild and spectacular.

The terrain is big and open, with couloirs and wide slopes around Toubkal and the surrounding peaks. Tours from the refuge offer a few days of varied skiing, with views of the Sahara on clear days.
highatlas.beyond: Imlil and the surrounding Berber villages offer warm hospitality, tagines and mint tea. The Kasbah du Toubkal is a famous lodge with views of the mountain. Marrakech is close for a city day.
highatlas.know:
Marrakech is about 2 hours from Imlil. A licensed local guide is required in Toubkal National Park.

There's no avalanche forecast. Snow conditions vary a lot, so check before you go.

sierranevada.skiing:
Sierra Nevada is Europe's southernmost major ski resort, with slopes up to the Veleta (3,396 m) and views across to Africa on clear days. The terrain is wide and open, with lots of sunny, intermediate pistes. It hosted the Alpine World Ski Championships in 1996.

The sun is strong, so mornings can be icy and afternoons slushy.

The resort, at Pradollano, has around 100 km of pistes, mostly sunny and intermediate. On clear days, the views stretch from the Mediterranean to the mountains of North Africa.
sierranevada.beyond: Granada and the Alhambra are about 1 hour away, and in Granada's bars, a tapa comes free with every drink. The Costa Tropical, on the Mediterranean, is about 1.5 hours away, so you can ski in the morning and swim in the afternoon in spring.
sierranevada.know:
Granada airport is about 1 hour away; Málaga is about 2 hours. Weekends and Spanish holidays are busy.

Off-piste is uncontrolled. Mulhacén, the highest peak in mainland Spain, is a ski-touring objective nearby.

crete.skiing:
Crete's White Mountains (Lefka Ori) rise to about 2,450 m, with a high, lunar karst plateau that offers ski touring in a setting like nowhere else in Europe, with the Libyan Sea glittering below. Psiloritis (Mount Ida), in the centre of the island, is the other option.

The snow is variable, but in a good winter, the touring is unforgettable.

The plateau is made of limestone, with sinkholes, ridges and long, open slopes. Touring days often end with views of the sea and a drive down to a village taverna.
crete.beyond: Psiloritis is the mythical birthplace of Zeus, in a cave on its slopes. Chania has a beautiful Venetian harbour. Cretan food, raki and tavernas by the beach are part of every day.
crete.know:
Chania airport is about 1.5 hours away. The Kallergi refuge, run by the local mountaineering club, is a base in the White Mountains.

There's no avalanche forecast. Check snow conditions before going.

Local guides run trips in good winters. Snow is very variable, so plan flexible dates.

etna.skiing:
Mount Etna, Europe's most active volcano, offers ski touring above the Mediterranean through steaming vents and black ash, with two small ski areas: **Etna Sud**, at Nicolosi, and **Etna Nord**, at Piano Provenzana. Touring from the lifts takes you up to near the summit craters.

The snow can be dusted with black ash from eruptions, which makes for surreal skiing.

The lifts are small and simple, but touring opens up big, open slopes and long descents toward the sea. On clear days, the views stretch across Sicily.
etna.beyond: Catania, at the foot of the volcano, has excellent street food: arancini and granita. Taormina, on the coast, has views of Etna, and the volcano's slopes produce some of Italy's most interesting wines.
etna.know:
Catania airport is about 1 hour away. Access to the summit area is regulated by the civil protection authorities, and guides are required above certain altitudes.

Eruptions can close areas at short notice. Check the latest volcanic activity before going.

afriski.skiing:
Afriski, in Lesotho's Maluti Mountains, is one of only two ski resorts in Southern Africa, at about 3,000 m. The terrain is small (a single main run of about 1 km), and most of the snow comes from snowmaking, but the experience of skiing in Africa is unique.

The season is short, roughly June to August.
afriski.beyond: Lesotho is called the "Kingdom in the Sky": it's the only country in the world entirely above 1,000 m. Basotho people wear distinctive woollen blankets and ride ponies in the mountains. The dramatic Sani Pass, further south, has the "highest pub in Africa" at the top.
afriski.know:
Johannesburg is about 5 to 6 hours by car. The roads are mountainous, so a 4x4 is useful.

The snow is mostly man-made, so check conditions before going.

Afriski has a lodge and chalets, and is popular with South African families. A trip can combine skiing with hiking or pony trekking in the highlands.

corsica.skiing:
The Alta Strada is a ski-touring traverse along the granite spine of Corsica, roughly following the GR20 hiking trail, with sea views on both sides. It takes about a week, staying in mountain refuges and shepherds' huts (*bergeries*). Monte Cinto (2,706 m), the island's highest peak, is on the way.

The snow is very variable, and the route depends on a good winter.

The terrain mixes granite ridges, open bowls and couloirs, with descents above the sea. In a good year, it's one of the most unusual hut traverses in Europe.
corsica.beyond: Corsican food is a highlight: brocciu cheese, charcuterie and chestnut dishes. The coast, with its beaches and villages, is close for days off.
corsica.know:
Bastia and Ajaccio have airports; ferries come from Nice, Marseille and Livorno. The refuges are mostly unstaffed in winter, so go with a guide or carry everything.

Météo-France publishes an avalanche bulletin for Corsica.

Most people do it with a guide, who can adapt the route to the snow. Late winter and spring are the best times.

sochi.skiing:
The resorts of Krasnaya Polyana, above Sochi, were built or rebuilt for the 2014 Winter Olympics. **Rosa Khutor**, which hosted the alpine events, has big modern lifts and long runs, and **Gazprom** (Laura and Alpika) and **Gorki Gorod** add more terrain. There's lots of tree skiing and sidecountry, and the snow can be deep, though it's often heavy and wet.

The base is low, so conditions vary with altitude.

Rosa Khutor's terrain is big, with long runs from about 2,300 m and a good mix of pistes and trees. The resorts are linked by gondolas and buses.
sochi.beyond: The Black Sea coast, with palm trees, is about an hour away. The Olympic Park in Adler has the old venues. Georgian and Caucasian food is excellent.
sochi.know:
Check your government's travel advice: many Western governments advise against all travel to Russia, and bank cards issued abroad don't work there.

Sochi airport is about 1 hour away. Fog and heavy snow can close lifts. Off-piste is uncontrolled.

elbrusarea.skiing:
The Elbrus region, in the Baksan valley, has huge, cheap freeride under Europe's highest peak. **Cheget** has old Soviet lifts and steep, varied terrain with views of the Donguz-Orun face. **Elbrus**, on the other side of the valley, has a modern cable car to about 3,850 m, with wide open slopes and big views.

The terrain is big and largely uncontrolled.

Cheget's freeride is steep and varied, with long, open descents through forest and couloirs. Elbrus's slopes are wide and high, with spectacular views of the Caucasus.
elbrusarea.beyond: The Balkar people live in the valley; try *khychiny*, thin pies filled with cheese and potato. The villages of Terskol and Cheget have simple hotels and cafés.
elbrusarea.know:
Check your government's travel advice: many Western governments advise against all travel to Russia, and specifically to the North Caucasus. Bank cards issued abroad don't work there.

Mineralnye Vody is about 3 hours away. There's no public avalanche forecast in English; go with a local guide.

elbrus.skiing:
Mount Elbrus (5,642 m), a dormant volcano with two summits, is the highest peak in Europe, and skiing from the top is one of the world's great volcano descents. The route goes up the south side, from the top of the cable car to the barrel huts at Garabashi and on to the summit.

The skiing isn't technical, but the altitude, cold and wind make it serious.
elbrus.beyond: The Baksan valley and the Caucasus mountains are spectacular. The barrel huts, converted from fuel tanks, are a famous part of the experience.
elbrus.know:
Check your government's travel advice: many Western governments advise against all travel to Russia, and specifically to the North Caucasus. Bank cards issued abroad don't work there.

Spring (roughly April to June) is the season. Acclimatise properly. Whiteouts on the summit plateau have killed many climbers.

Trips usually take about a week, with acclimatisation climbs and a summit day. Snowcats can take you part of the way, which helps with the long summit day.

dombai.skiing:
Dombai sits under dramatic Caucasus peaks like Dombai-Ulgen (4,046 m), with old lifts and big off-piste. **Arkhyz**, nearby, is a fast-growing modern resort, with new lifts and wide pistes.

Both are cheap, and the off-piste is big and largely uncontrolled.

Dombai's terrain is steep and dramatic, with views of glaciers and needle-like peaks. Arkhyz is gentler and newer, with modern gondolas and a growing village. Freeriders come for the huge, untracked off-piste around both.
dombai.beyond: The Teberda Nature Reserve surrounds Dombai. Near Arkhyz, tenth-century Alanian churches and a large Soviet telescope, once the largest in the world, are interesting stops.
dombai.know:
Check your government's travel advice: many Western governments advise against all travel to Russia, and specifically to the North Caucasus. Bank cards issued abroad don't work there.

Mineralnye Vody is about 4 hours away. There's no public avalanche forecast in English.

Infrastructure is improving but still basic in places, and English is rarely spoken. Go with an operator who knows the area.

khibiny.skiing:
The Khibiny Mountains, on the Kola Peninsula above the Arctic Circle, offer Arctic freeride and touring: open bowls, cirques and long spring days. The resort of Bolshoy Vudyavr, above Kirovsk, has modern lifts and big terrain.

The season is long, running into June, and in May the sun barely sets.

The terrain includes open bowls, steep chutes and long valley runs, with views over frozen lakes. Touring from Kirovsk opens up big terrain in the surrounding cirques.
khibiny.beyond: Kirovsk and Apatity are mining towns, named for the apatite mined here. In winter, a snow village with ice sculptures and a snow hotel opens in Kirovsk. The northern lights are common in the dark months.
khibiny.know:
Check your government's travel advice: many Western governments advise against all travel to Russia, and bank cards issued abroad don't work there.

Apatity airport is about 30 minutes away. The Khibiny has one of Russia's oldest avalanche services, because of the mining.

sheregesh.skiing:
Sheregesh, in the Gornaya Shoria region of Siberia, is famous for its deep, very cold, dry snow in birch and fir forests. The trees are often coated with snow and rime, and the tree skiing can be excellent.

The terrain is mostly moderate, but the snow quality is the draw.

The resort, on Mount Zelenaya, has several lift areas around a single peak, with lots of tree skiing and sidecountry between them. Many skiers come for the off-piste, where the snow stays light for days after a storm in the cold.
sheregesh.beyond: Sheregesh is known for its spring party, the Grelka Fest, where skiers ride in swimsuits. The Shor people are the indigenous inhabitants of the area.
sheregesh.know:
Check your government's travel advice: many Western governments advise against all travel to Russia, and bank cards issued abroad don't work there.

Novokuznetsk is about 3 hours away. Midwinter can be extremely cold, below −30 °C.

The resort is popular with Russian skiers and snowboarders, and weekends can be busy. English is rarely spoken.

kamchatka.skiing:
Kamchatka, in Russia's far east, offers heli-skiing on volcanoes that run down to the Pacific. It's one of the wildest heli destinations on Earth, with huge open slopes, steaming craters and descents that end at the ocean.

The terrain is big and remote, and the volcanoes are active.

Typical descents run 1,000 to 2,000 m, from the shoulders of volcanoes like Vilyuchinsky and Mutnovsky down to the coast, and the open, treeless slopes in spring give long corn runs. The volcanoes steam, the sea glitters, and there's rarely another person in sight.
kamchatka.beyond: Kamchatka has hot springs, geysers and brown bears. The Valley of Geysers is one of the largest geyser fields in the world.
kamchatka.know:
Check your government's travel advice: many Western governments advise against all travel to Russia, and bank cards issued abroad don't work there.

Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky is the nearest airport. Heli-skiing is weather-dependent, so allow for down days.

Trips are usually sold as a week, run by a few operators. Old Soviet helicopters are often used. Spring (March to May) brings longer days and more stable snow.
